summary: Research and fact-check the science behind "Why the Best Players Look Slow" (scanning, first touch physics, body shape, reaction time) plus coaching cues, drills and a topic challenge

research.topic: LOOK: scanning (visual exploratory activity) before receiving the ball
research.one_line_hook: The best players are not faster than you. They finished looking before the ball arrived, so with the ball they have nothing left to do but play.
research.mechanism_story:
Picture Tavi waiting for a pass on the night pitch. The ball is 15 metres away and rolling toward her. Right now she has the most free time she will get all night. Chalk, the chalk keeper who now chases, is somewhere behind her. If she waits until the ball reaches her foot to find out where, it is already too late. Here is why.

Her eyes see sharp detail only in a tiny spot, about the size of a thumbnail held at arm's length. Everything else is blurry side-vision. Side-vision is good at catching movement, but bad at telling a teammate from an opponent. And her eyes cannot see behind her at all. The only way to know what is behind is to turn her head. Scientists call that a scan: a quick head turn away from the ball to check the pitch, then back.

A scan is fast. Eye-tracking glasses on pro midfielders show a normal scan takes about four tenths of a second. Nine out of ten last less than two thirds of a second. The eyes almost never stop to stare. The head swings out, pauses for a blink, and swings back. In that blink the player takes a rough snapshot: about one to three teammates, one to three opponents, and the gaps between them.

Those snapshots go into a small mental map. The map is small because working memory holds only about four things at once. And it goes stale fast, because everyone keeps moving. So the best players refresh it again and again. Premier League players scan roughly once every two seconds while their team has the ball, and they turn their heads faster and faster as the pass gets close. Top midfielders such as Lampard and Gerrard were measured at about six scans in ten seconds.

Now the payoff. When something new appears, the brain needs about a quarter of a second just to react, and more time to decide. A defender needs about the same. If Tavi already knows Chalk is closing from her left, she has no reaction left to do. Her first touch already goes right, into space. That is the time bubble: the looks she took before the ball arrived turn into seconds with the ball.

The data agrees. In the Premier League study, players who scanned most completed about 73 percent of their passes. Players who scanned least completed 54 percent. For midfielders passing forward, the gap was 38 percent against 73 percent. Looking early does not make you faster. It makes you early. And early looks slow.
plain_metaphors: A scan is a camera snapshot, not a video. Click, and back to the ball. Pros take a snapshot in about 0.4 seconds.
Your sharp vision is a torch beam in a dark room. The beam is narrow. You must move the torch (turn your head) to see what is behind you.
Your mental map is a whiteboard with four sticky notes. Old notes fall off as players move. Scanning sticks fresh notes on.
Scanning is checking the mirrors before you change lane. You check before you move, not while you are already moving.
The time bubble is a shrinking ring. Every look you take before the ball arrives makes the ring bigger when the ball is at your feet.
Looking after the ball arrives is like reading the exam question after the timer starts. The clock (about a quarter of a second to react, plus deciding) is already running.
Peripheral vision is a smoke alarm. It tells you something moved. It cannot tell you which shirt colour moved.

jargon_map.term: Scan (visual exploratory activity, VEA, exploratory search)
jargon_map.plain_version: A quick head turn away from the ball to look around, then back to the ball. Researchers count these on video.
How many looks you take in the seconds before the ball reaches you. 0.5 per second means one look every two seconds.

jargon_map.term: Head turn frequency / head turn excursion (IMU studies)
jargon_map.plain_version: Head turns counted by a motion sensor in a headband, and how far the head swings. Sensors count more turns than video does, so the numbers are not the same as scans.
The eyes stopping on one thing for at least about a tenth of a second. During most scans the eyes do not stop at all.
The moment the head reaches the far end of the turn, just before it comes back. That is where most of the useful picture is taken.
The tiny sharp centre of what you see, about 1.5 to 2 degrees wide.
The blurry side-vision. Good at spotting movement, bad at detail.
Everything your two eyes can see at once without moving your head: about 200 degrees wide, a bit more than a half circle. Nothing behind you.
The small notepad in your head that holds about four things at once.
The time from seeing something to starting to move: about a quarter of a second in adults.
Deciding what you will do before the ball arrives, so the first touch is already a decision.
Parking your eyes in a smart spot so side-vision can watch several things at once, or so the next look is short.
How close the nearest defender is. Under tight pressure players scan less, because there is no time.
The old Sky Sports split-screen feed that follows one player. Jordet used it to count scans in 2013.
Standing sideways to the passer so you can see the ball and the pitch at the same time. It also makes each scan a shorter turn.

claims.claim: Original definition of a scan (visual exploration) used in the 2013 Premier League study: 'A body and/or head movement in which the player's face is actively and temporarily directed away from the ball, seemingly with the intention of looking for teammates, opponents or other environmental objects or events, relevant to perform a subsequent action with the ball.' Counted in the 10 s before the player received the ball.
claims.value: head/body turn away from the ball; 10-s window before reception

claims.claim: Jordet, Bloomfield & Heijmerikx (2013, MIT Sloan) sample: 118 Premier League midfielders and forwards, 1,279 situations, 64 games, filmed with Sky PlayerCam. Inter-observer agreement on scan counts was 72%.

Population: Premier League pros (2013). Mean scan frequency was 0.33 scans/s for players who had won a major individual award and 0.27 scans/s for the others. The two highest individual averages were Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard, both 0.62 scans/s. So '0.6 scans/s' is a top-player number, not a Premier League average.
claims.value: 0.33 vs 0.27 scans/s; Lampard and Gerrard 0.62 scans/s

claims.claim: Population: Premier League pros (2013). Pass completion by scan-frequency band: 53.7% (0-0.20 scans/s), 61.0% (0.21-0.40, OR 1.35), 72.6% (0.41-1.80, OR 2.29). For midfielders' forward passes: 38.2% completed with little scanning vs 73.2% with much scanning (OR 4.42).

Jordet et al. (2020, Frontiers in Psychology) definition: a scan is 'a player's active head movement where the face (and hence, the eyes) is temporarily directed away from the ball'. Sample: 27 professional players (17-32 y) from one Premier League club, 21 matches, 9,574 ball possessions, measured in the last 10 s before reception.
Population: Premier League pros (2020). Mean scan frequency 0.44 scans/s (SD 0.30). Central midfielders scanned most, then central defenders, wingers, full-backs; forwards least (d = 0.55).

Population: Premier League pros (2020). Controlling for pass difficulty in a Bayesian model, more scanning raised the probability of completing a pass (mu-beta = 0.13, credible interval 0.02-0.24). Players scanned more before long or forward passes than short or backward ones (d = 0.19-0.24), and scanned 0.46 scans/s when possession was kept vs 0.37 when it was lost (d = 0.20).

Population: Premier League pros (2020). Scanning was lowest when the nearest opponent was 0-1 m away and rose with distance up to about 4 m, after which it stopped increasing. Scanning was high in the own penalty area and central channels, and dropped in the attacking third, near both six-yard boxes and near the sidelines.

McGuckian et al. (2018, 'Don't Turn Blind!'): 32 semi-elite Australian NPL players (16-30 y, mean 19.0), 11v11, head-mounted inertial sensor at 250 Hz. A head turn = rotation about the vertical axis faster than 125 deg/s. Note: this counts turns toward and away from the ball, so numbers are higher than video 'scans'.

Population: semi-elite adults (McGuckian 2018). Head-turn rate rose as the ball approached: 0.95 turns/s over the full 10 s before possession vs 1.44 turns/s in the final 1 s. Higher head-turn frequency 2-9 s before possession raised the odds of a forward pass. Bigger head swings (excursion) raised the odds of turning with the ball and of passing to the opposite side (about 2-3x). Neither measure predicted pass success in this study.

McGuckian et al. (2019, Ecological Psychology) lab task: experienced players 'received' a simulated ball surrounded by 4 targets with 1, 2 or 3 s to explore. Higher head-movement frequency predicted faster passing responses. This is the direct evidence that looking before the ball arrives buys time with the ball.

Population: youth (McGuckian et al. 2020, J Sports Sci). 22 competitive-elite youth players, mean age 16.25 y, 1,623 minutes of 11v11 with head sensors. Players explored more when in possession, least during transitions, most in the back third and least in the middle third.

Population: U13 and U23 (McGuckian et al. 2020, Science and Medicine in Football). 14 U13 and 14 U23 players from a Bundesliga club in the Footbonaut. More head turns before ball contact predicted faster completion; the exact pattern differed between U13 and U23.

Aksum et al. (2020, eye tracking in 11v11): 5 elite Norwegian midfielders (17-23 y), 2,832 fixations analysed. Mean fixation duration 242 ms (SD 195, range 120-2,400 ms). Players spent most viewing time on the player in possession, then on ball/opponents/teammates.

Aksum et al. (2021, PLOS ONE): 4 elite Norwegian central midfielders, 869 scans with eye-tracking glasses. Mean scan duration 0.40 s (median 0.34 s, SD 0.28); 90.3% of scans lasted 0.66 s or less; the most common duration was 0.26 s. So one look costs well under half a second.

Population: elite pros (Aksum 2021, PLOS ONE). Only 20 of 869 scans (2.3%) contained a fixation of 120 ms or more. Scans with a fixation averaged 0.97 s; scans without averaged 0.38 s. The authors conclude that players do not need to stop and stare during a scan to get useful information.

Population: elite pros (Aksum 2021, PLOS ONE). Scans were longer when the ball was in the air (0.45 s vs 0.38 s on the ground) and when the ball was travelling between players (0.44 s) than when a player had it under control between touches (0.35 s). Players look longer when the ball's path is predictable.

Population: elite pros (Aksum 2021, PLOS ONE). At the stop point of a scan the video frame most often held 1-3 teammates and 1-3 opponents; players had more opponents than teammates in view, especially in attack. Practical advice from the authors: most scans are shorter than 0.5 s, so coaches should limit non-football information such as counting fingers or reading a number, and link scans to a real decision (turn, pass, dribble).

Population: elite youth (Aksum, Pokolm, Bjørndal, Rein, Memmert & Jordet 2021, J Sports Sci). 53 outfield players from the 2018 UEFA U17 and U19 Championship semi-finals and finals, 1,686 attacking situations. U19 players scanned more than U17 players; scan frequency was positively related to pass success; central midfielders and central defenders scanned most; opponent pressure and pitch position mattered. Exact scans/s values are in the paywalled full text and were not verified here.

Pokolm et al. (2022, J Sport Exerc Psychol): 239 players in 17 UEFA U17/U19/U21 Championship matches (2018-2019). Scanning frequency was positively related to successful passes and to changes in body orientation, and to national-team appearances. Opponent pressure had a large effect on pass result.

Population: elite youth women, 17.45 +/- 0.88 y (Abächerli et al. 2026). 39 players, 819 events in 11v11 championship matches. Scan frequency before reception 0.27 +/- 0.22 scans/s; during possession 0.61 +/- 0.45 scans/s; average possession lasted only 1.62 +/- 0.95 s. Each extra 0.1 scans/s during possession raised the odds of a completed pass by 9% (OR 1.09). Pre-reception scan frequency and the timing of scans in four 2.5-s windows were not significant predictors, though the last 2.5 s trended highest for successful passes.

Population: elite youth women, 17.6 +/- 0.7 y (Hintermann et al. 2025, EJSS). In 4v4 games, verbal cues raised scans per possession from 0.99 to 1.14 (+27%, rate ratio 1.27, CI 1.12-1.44). Possessions with at least one scan before reception were far more likely to end well (OR 3.40, CI 2.59-4.62). Cues used: 'Before you receive the ball, see where your open teammates are positioned', 'Locate the opponents' positions before your first touch', 'Check your surroundings for open spaces before you get the ball'.
claims.value: +27% scans; OR 3.40 for a good outcome after >= 1 scan

claims.claim: Population: youth women, 16.7 +/- 1.2 y, elite and grassroots (Hintermann et al. 2025, 'Heads Up Girls!'). A 5-week programme (1-2 sessions/week, a 30-min block of scanning games and passing exercises after the warm-up) raised scans per game situation from 0.88 to 1.44 in the intervention group vs 0.61 to 0.92 in controls (partial eta-squared 0.20). The gain was significant only in elite players (1.06 -> 1.72), not grassroots (0.52 -> 0.87).

Population: U16-U17 boys, 16.77 +/- 0.42 y (Erişik et al. 2025, randomized). 22 players; 7 weeks of VR drills 3x/week. Scans before reception rose from 18 to 43 in the VR group (controls -12% to +37% across measures); one-touch short passes +38% and penetrative passes +108%.

Population: elite academy boys aged 13 (Tiercery et al. 2025, preprint). 16 players; four 20-min VR sessions. Scanning frequency rose 49% in the VR group vs -2% in controls, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.13). Passing accuracy did not change.

Population: U15 boys (Praça et al. 2026). 35 players in 3v3 games. Off-ball head movements away from the ball were more frequent in successful defensive sequences (0.267 per s) than unsuccessful ones (0.152 per s), d = 0.55. Scanning matters when defending too.

Population: youth central midfielders, training games (Eldridge, Pulling & Robins 2013). 3 players, five 20-min games. When they scanned before receiving they played more forward passes, more passes into the attacking half, turned more often and faced less defensive pressure (p < 0.01).
claims.value: more forward passes and turns after scanning

claims.claim: Pocock, Dicks, Thelwell, Chapman & Barker (2019, J Applied Sport Psychology): 5 elite academy players; a 6-week PETTLEP imagery programme (single-case multiple-baseline design) increased visual exploratory activity, most clearly in centre midfielders, with some signs of better on-ball performance. Ages of the players were not verified (abstract only).

Jordet (2005): imagery training with 3 elite players; 2 of 3 increased their scanning and 1 of 3 marginally improved performance with the ball. Together with Pocock 2019 and the 2025 youth programmes, this shows scanning is trainable, but the transfer to better passing is smaller and less certain.

Population: Euro 2016 midfielders, adults (Phatak & Gruber 2019). 35 players. Scan rate correlated positively with passing percentage (p = 0.033, R-squared 3.0%; total scans p = 0.015, R-squared 4.0%); transition scans correlated negatively with turnover rate (p = 0.023, R-squared 3.5%). Scanning explains only up to about 4% of the variance, so it is one factor among many.

Population: elite women, mean 26.7 y (Feist et al. 2024, Women's Euro 2022). 30 central midfielders, 1,038 possessions. Mean scan frequency before receiving 0.35 scans/s, lower than reported for men's elite and academy players; pitch location was the main predictor of scan frequency.

Simple visual reaction time in adults is about 0.21-0.24 s (231 ms raw, 213 ms after hardware correction in 1,469 adults; 238 ms in a second sample). Stimulus detection alone took about 131 ms. Any decision adds time on top. Values for 12-16 year olds were not verified; they are usually a little slower than adults.

Working memory holds about four chunks at once (Cowan 2001, Behavioral and Brain Sciences), with the wider literature saying three to five. A player's mental map of the pitch is therefore small and must be refreshed often.

Review of peripheral vision in sport (Vater, Williams & Hossner 2020): athletes use a 'gaze anchor' (park the eyes in one spot and monitor cues with peripheral vision, which avoids information loss during eye jumps under time pressure) or a 'visual pivot' (a spot between cues from which short eye movements reach each cue).

The combined human visual field is about 200-220 degrees wide and 130-135 degrees tall; foveal (sharp) vision covers only the central 1.5-2 degrees; peripheral vision is good at detecting motion but weak at detail, colour and shape. Nothing behind the player is visible without a head turn.

FOLKLORE CHECK: 'Xavi scans 0.83 times per second' comes from Geir Jordet's own unpublished filming, reported in media (Sky Sports, 10 Nov 2017, Ben Lyttleton) and on Jordet's X account, not from a peer-reviewed paper. The same Sky article gives Lampard 0.62 and Gerrard 0.61, and quotes Jordet that 'anything over 0.50 visual searches per second is very high'.

FOLKLORE CHECK: the Sky Sports article reports 81% vs 64% pass completion (most vs least scanning) and 75% vs 41% for forward passes. These do not match the 2013 MIT Sloan paper (72.6% vs 53.7%; 73.2% vs 38.2% for midfielders' forward passes), so they likely come from a different or later Jordet dataset. Use the paper's numbers.

Jordet's X post (Oct 2021) as quoted in search snippets: 'Of all players we have filmed these past 20+ years, Xavi Hernández is the one with the highest average frequency in a full game: 0.83 scans per second.' The post itself could not be fetched here.
Xavi's own words (Guardian interview by Sid Lowe, 11 Feb 2011, as quoted in Jordet 2013): 'Think, think, think. Quickly... Lift your head up, move, see, think. Look before you get the ball.'

The FA (England Football Learning, 'What is receiving in football?', 1 Oct 2021): 'Second, the receiving player must scan the pitch.' 'So, when working on receiving, start by highlighting the importance of looking around.' 'Glancing at opponents, teammates, and the available space will help your players make their next decision.'

The FA ('How to coach players on receiving in football', 12 Oct 2021) teaches receiving through questions before the ball arrives: 'Where's the defender?', 'Where are my teammates moving?', 'What space can I use?', 'How should you position your body to see more of the pitch?'. The FA does not use the phrase 'check your shoulder' on these pages; it says 'scan', 'look around' and 'take a picture'.

FA session 'Receiving skills: take a picture' (Pete Sturgess, early-years/foundation phase): small-sided 3v3 to 5v5; players 'open up their body when receiving the ball' so they are 'better able to look at the player in possession and scan the rest of the pitch', which 'helps them make better decisions'. Progression: shrink the area slowly (STEP).

US Youth Soccer 'Skills School: Key Coaching Points of Each Major Technique' (Coaching Education Dept, Sam Snow). Its receiving points say 'watch the ball onto the receiving foot' and 'eyes on the ball'; it does not list a pre-receive shoulder check. Scanning appears under running with the ball ('the head is up and the eyes scan the field') and running ('turn the head only when needed to tactically scan the field'). No official US Youth Soccer 'check your shoulder' page was found.
claims.value: official US manual: scan while running, not stated for receiving

claims.claim: KNVB and UEFA: no official KNVB (incl. Rinus) or UEFA web page on scanning could be found or fetched in this session. The KNVB Rinus training-content page lists 'aannemen' (receiving) but does not mention scanning. Treat any 'KNVB teaches kijken-denken-doen for scanning' line as unverified.

Coaching convention (not from a governing body): 'scan before you receive the ball, not when it has already reached you'; take the look 'when you see the ball leaving his foot'. The 'two-scan' version (one look as the ball leaves the passer's foot, a second just before it arrives) is common coaching folklore; the research support is indirect (head-turn rate peaks in the last second, and scans are longer while the ball travels).
claims.value: first look as the ball leaves the foot

claims.claim: Classic partner drill ('Passing Y'): Player A passes to B; C stands behind B in the blind spot. 'As the ball leaves A's foot, Player C holds up a number of fingers (1-5). Player B must scan over their shoulder, spot the number, and shout it out before controlling the ball.' Progressions: colour signals that decide the turn direction, one-touch. Note Aksum et al. 2021 warn that finger-counting is non-football information; use it briefly, then switch to real cues (a defender's position).

technique_cues: Ball leaves the foot, head goes. The first look starts the moment the passer strikes it.
Snapshot, not a stare. Half a second, then eyes back to the ball for the touch.
Refresh before it arrives. The map goes stale in two seconds, so take a second look late in the ball's flight.
Find the wrong shirt first. The nearest opponent decides your first touch. Teammates come second.
Open the door. Stand side-on to the passer so the look is a small turn, not a full spin.
Look with a plan. Every look answers one question: turn, pass or protect?
Eyes back for the touch. Watch the ball onto the foot, then look up again.
Under tight pressure, look earlier. If a defender is within a metre you will not get a look with the ball, so take it while the ball travels.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ball-watching: eyes glued to the ball for the whole pass.
common_mistakes.consequence: The player finds the defender only after the first touch. Reaction plus decision costs half a second or more, and the time bubble collapses. In the Premier League data the lowest scanners completed 54% of passes versus 73% for the highest.
common_mistakes.fix: Cue 'ball leaves the foot, head goes'. Start with the Passing Y (call the fingers), then replace the fingers with a real defender's position.

common_mistakes.mistake: One early look, then nothing. Scanning 5 seconds before the pass and never again.
common_mistakes.consequence: Players move. The mental map holds about four items and is out of date by the time the ball arrives. Head-turn rate in good players actually peaks in the final second before reception.
common_mistakes.fix: Two-beat habit: one look as the ball leaves the passer's foot, one more late in the flight. Film 10-second clips from behind and count the looks.

common_mistakes.mistake: Staring instead of snapshotting: a long look of a second or more.
common_mistakes.consequence: The ball arrives while the head is turned. First touch fails or the ball is stolen. Pro scans average 0.4 s and almost never include a fixation.
common_mistakes.fix: Practise 'click and back' with a wall: glance at a cone behind you and return before the rebound. Shorten the turn by receiving side-on.

common_mistakes.mistake: Scanning only when you have the ball, especially under pressure.
common_mistakes.consequence: With an opponent within a metre, pros scan the least because there is no time. A look with the ball at your feet under pressure invites a tackle.
common_mistakes.fix: Move the looking earlier, to the moment the ball is travelling. With the ball, use short glances between touches, and only when the nearest defender is 2 metres or more away.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking only for friends.
common_mistakes.consequence: The nearest opponent, not the open teammate, decides whether the first touch is safe. Elite midfielders have more opponents than teammates in view during scans.
common_mistakes.fix: Cue 'wrong shirt first'. In drills, make the receiver call the side the defender is on, then touch away from it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Square body to the passer.
common_mistakes.consequence: Every look needs a big turn, so the player takes fewer looks and loses the ball from view for longer.
common_mistakes.fix: Receive half-turned so ball and most of the pitch sit inside the roughly 200-degree visual field, and the look behind is a short turn.

common_mistakes.mistake: Scanning without a decision (looking because the coach said so).
common_mistakes.consequence: The look does not change the next action, so it buys no time. Researchers found scanning explains only a few percent of pass success on its own; it works when it drives the touch.
common_mistakes.fix: Pair every look with a call before the ball arrives: 'turn', 'back' or 'bounce'. Reward the correct decision, not the head movement.

drills: Wall snapshot (alone). Stand 5-6 m from a wall with three coloured cones or shirts spread behind you. Pass firmly against the wall. As the ball leaves your foot, turn your head, say the colour of the cone nearest to a chosen mark (for example the goal), and get your eyes back before the rebound. Control it and go again. Ten passes each side. Safety: use a solid wall with no windows, make sure nobody is behind you, and clear the ground of stones.

Two-look wall drill (alone). Same setup, but take two short looks: one as the ball leaves your foot, one when it bounces off the wall. Call one colour on each look. Keep each look under half a second; if the ball gets past you, the look was too long. Safety: start with soft passes, add pace only when the timing is clean.

Moving-defender receive (with one friend). Friend passes from 10 m and then jogs to your left, right or behind you at random. While the ball travels, take one look, then take your first touch away from the side the friend went to. Swap after 10 passes. Progress to the friend arriving as a real, gentle defender. Safety: agree no tackles, only a shadow at arm's length, and use a flat grass area.

Passing Y with fingers, one friend and a phone (with one friend). Set a phone on a bench behind you playing a random-number video or put a stack of numbered cards face down. Friend passes; as the ball leaves the foot you turn, read the number or the card the friend flipped, shout it, and control the ball. Do 20, then switch the number for a real cue: the friend calls 'left' or 'right' and you must turn the other way. Safety: keep the phone or cards well behind the ball path.

Side-on receive shuttle (with one friend). Mark two gates 8 m apart. Receive every pass half-turned so you can see the passer and the gate you must play through. Before each pass, the friend silently points to one gate; you must find it with one look during the pass and play into it with two touches. Safety: gates 2 m wide, no slide tackles.

Ten-second count (alone with a phone). Film yourself from behind during a small-sided game or practice. Count head turns away from the ball in the 10 s before each time you receive. Aim to move from under 3 to 4-6 per 10 s, which matches good pro numbers. Safety: none beyond normal play; ask before filming others.

Juggle and glance (alone). While juggling, glance up every third touch and say something you see (a tree, a friend, the goal). Keep the ball up. This trains quick eyes-off-ball moments without stress. Safety: soft ground, no roads nearby.
animation_ideas: Time bubble ring: a glowing ring around Tavi labelled in seconds (distance to Chalk divided by his closing speed). Each pre-pass scan adds a visible slice of time; a missed scan shows the ring shrinking to zero as the ball arrives.

Polaroid scans: every head turn spits out a small polaroid of what she saw (1-3 teammates, 1-3 opponents, a gap). The photos pin to a whiteboard with only four slots; old photos fade and fall off as players move.

Torch-beam vision: a dark pitch where Tavi's sharp vision is a narrow torch beam and side-vision is a dim 200-degree glow. Chalk creeps in from behind, outside the glow, until the head turns and the beam catches him.
Stopwatch on a scan: slow-motion head turn with a stopwatch counting 0.00 to 0.40 s, freeze at the stop point with the caption 'snapshot taken', then the head snaps back before the ball arrives.
Head-turn rate ramp: a 10-second bar above the travelling ball with tick marks for head turns, sparse at 10 s and dense in the last second (0.95/s to 1.44/s), like a Geiger counter speeding up.

Reaction-time race: split screen. Left, Tavi who scanned takes a first touch away from Chalk at 0.00 s. Right, Tavi who did not scan: a 0.25 s 'seeing' bar, then a 'deciding' bar, then Chalk's chalk hand already on the ball.
Pass-completion bar chart in chalk: three chalk bars drawn on the night pitch, 54%, 61%, 73%, labelled by looks per 10 seconds (0-2, 2-4, 4+), then the midfielder forward-pass version 38% vs 73%.

PlayerCam homage: a retro split-screen where the small window shows the wide game and the big window follows only Tavi, with a scan counter ticking in the corner and Sam's off-ball run appearing in the small window before she 'sees' it.
Pressure dimmer: as Chalk closes from 4 m to 1 m, the scan counter dims to almost zero, showing why the looks must happen while the ball is still travelling.

Xavi caption card: a chalk 'folklore meter' that stamps '0.83 scans/s: media, not paper' next to '0.62: Lampard and Gerrard, published', with the Xavi quote 'Look before you get the ball' written in chalk.

mechanism_errors: 'Premier League players scan roughly once every two seconds while their team has the ball' mixes two studies and mislabels the window. Jordet 2020 (27 players, one club) found 0.44 scans/s, about one look every 2.3 s, measured only in the 10 s before the player received the ball. The 118-player 2013 sample averaged 0.27-0.33 scans/s, about one look every 3-4 s. Say 'once every two to three seconds in the seconds before they receive a pass'.

'they turn their heads faster and faster as the pass gets close' sits in the Premier League paragraph but comes from McGuckian 2018: 32 semi-elite Australian adults with head sensors, which count all head turns (0.95/s over 10 s → 1.44/s in the last second), not video scans. Name the population or move the sentence.

'the looks she took before the ball arrived turn into seconds with the ball' overstates the gain. The direct evidence (McGuckian 2019, lab task) is faster pass decisions, in tenths of a second. In elite U19 women's matches an average possession lasts only 1.62 s. Say 'a fraction of a second' or 'time'.

'Now the payoff ... The data agrees' presents the 2013 pass-completion numbers as a causal payoff. That study is correlational and did not control pass difficulty. Jordet 2020 controlled for difficulty and still found a positive link, but both are observational. Phatak & Gruber 2019 found scanning explains only 3-4% of the variance in pass completion. Phrase it as 'players who scanned more also completed more passes'.

'The map is small because working memory holds only about four things at once' is an analogy, not a tested finding. Cowan's 4-chunk limit comes from lab memory tasks. No scanning study measured a player's mental map. Jordet, McGuckian and Aksum use an ecological framing (scan to pick up information for the next action), not a stored map. Keep the line as a picture, not as science.
'The head swings out, pauses for a blink, and swings back' mildly conflicts with the finding that 97.7% of scans have no fixation at all. 'Pauses' is fine as metaphor, but do not say the eyes stop.

'a normal scan takes about four tenths of a second' comes from 4 Norwegian top-league central midfielders, not Premier League players. The story says 'pro midfielders', which is accurate, but avoid letting the audience assume it is the same Premier League group.

For U12 and U16 viewers, all headline numbers are from adult pros. Youth values are lower and possessions are shorter: elite U19 women 0.27 scans/s before reception and 1.62 s per possession; a 13-year-old academy group gained +49% scanning with VR but with no significant effect and no passing change. Name the population every time a number appears.

Pros (Premier League midfielders, 2013): forward passes were completed 73.2% of the time with much scanning and 38.2% with little scanning.
Pros (Premier League, 2013): Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard both averaged 0.62 scans per second, about six looks in ten seconds. Award-winning players averaged 0.33 scans/s, others 0.27.

Pros (27 players from one Premier League club, 2020): 0.44 scans per second in the ten seconds before receiving, about one look every two to three seconds. 0.46 scans/s when possession was kept vs 0.37 when it was lost.
Pros (4 Norwegian top-league central midfielders, eye-tracking): an average scan lasts 0.40 s; nine out of ten last 0.66 s or less; only 2.3% of scans contain a fixation.
Pros (same 4 midfielders): at the end of a scan the view most often holds one to three teammates and one to three opponents.
Semi-elite adults (32 Australian NPL players, head sensors): head turns rose from 0.95 per second over the ten seconds before the ball to 1.44 per second in the final second.
Elite youth women (39 players, 17.5 y, 11v11): an average possession lasts 1.62 s; every extra 0.1 scans per second during possession raised the odds of completing the pass by 9%.

Elite youth women (25 players, 17.6 y, 4v4): one sentence of coaching cue raised scans per possession by 27%; a possession with at least one scan before the ball arrived was 3.4 times more likely to end well.

Youth women (36 players, 16.7 y): a 5-week programme with a 30-min scanning block after the warm-up raised scans per situation from 0.88 to 1.44 (controls 0.61 to 0.92). The gain was significant only in elite players.
U16-U17 boys (22 players, randomized): 7 weeks of VR drills, three per week, raised scans before reception from 18 to 43 per game; one-touch short passes +38%.
U15 boys (35 players, 3v3): defenders made 0.267 off-ball head movements per second in successful defensive sequences vs 0.152 in unsuccessful ones (small study).
Adults (1,469 people): simple visual reaction time is about 0.21-0.24 s; detecting the stimulus alone takes about 0.13 s. Teenagers are a little slower.
Human vision: the two eyes together cover about 200-220 degrees; sharp detail covers only the central 1.5-2 degrees, about a thumbnail at arm's length.
Elite adult midfielders (35 players, Euro 2016): scanning explains only 3-4% of the variance in pass completion. It is one factor among many.
Elite women (30 central midfielders, Euro 2022): 0.35 scans per second before receiving, lower than men's elite and academy players.
Xavi 0.83 scans per second: Geir Jordet's own filming, reported by Sky Sports in 2017, not a peer-reviewed number. Jordet: 'anything over 0.50 visual searches per second is very high'.

research.topic: TOUCH: the physics and coaching of the first touch when receiving a ground pass (episode: "Why the Best Players Look Slow", chapter 2)
research.one_line_hook: A football does not bounce off your foot because your foot is hard. It bounces off the speed difference. Kill the difference and you buy metres, and every metre is a fifth of a second.
research.mechanism_story:
A pass is coming at Tavi at about ten metres per second. The ball does not care how fast it is going. It only cares about the speed difference between itself and Tavi's foot. That difference gets squashed into the ball for about nine thousandths of a second and then springs back out. A football is a good spring: dropped onto a steel plate it keeps more than 80 percent of its speed. A foot and ankle are a worse spring, because skin, boot and joint soak up energy, so a ball that hits a still, firm foot comes back with roughly half of its speed. Half of ten is five metres per second. On a good pitch the grass only steals about one metre per second every second, so that ball would roll about twelve metres before it stopped. That is the bounce-away touch, and Chalk gets there first.

Now Tavi does the pro thing. As the ball arrives, the foot is already moving back with it. The speed difference shrinks. If the foot moves back at about a third of the ball's speed, the small bounce and the foot's own motion cancel, and the ball just stops. Move the foot back a little less and the ball leaves at a jogging pace, about two metres per second. Grass brakes that in roughly two seconds and two metres. That is the touch into space.

Why bother with two metres? Because football is measured in the time the nearest defender needs to reach the ball. A defender who is already running closes about five to eight metres every second, so each metre of space is worth roughly a fifth of a second. A two-metre touch away from the defender, taken with the far foot across the body, buys nearly half a second, and the defender must also change direction. Half a second is enormous. A simple reaction takes about a quarter of a second. Top players hold the ball for about one second and two touches per possession.

So the first touch has three jobs at once. Look before the ball comes, so you know where the space is. Give with the foot, so the speed difference, not the ball, decides how far it goes. Send the ball to the spot where your next action starts, not to your own feet. Do that and you look slow, because you are the only one who is not in a hurry.
plain_metaphors: Catching an egg: your hands move back with the egg so the egg never feels a hard stop. A giving foot does the same to the ball.
Trampoline versus sandpit: a stiff, locked foot is a trampoline and throws the ball away; a relaxed foot that moves back is a sandpit and swallows the speed.
The ball is a spring. In a hard kick it squashes by about six centimetres and pushes back. Less speed difference means less squash and less push-back.
The speed-difference rule: a ball that lands on a moving train at train speed just sits there. Make your foot the train.
Grass is a soft brake pedal. It steals about one metre per second every second, so a two-metre-per-second touch stops after about two metres.
The time bubble: draw a ring around the player whose radius is seconds, not metres. Every metre of space adds about a fifth of a second to the ring.
Pinball flipper versus catcher's mitt: same ball, opposite result, and the only thing that changed is how the surface moves at the moment of contact.

jargon_map.plain_version: The bounciness number: how much of the speed difference comes back after a hit. About 0.8 for a ball on steel, about 0.5 for a ball on a kicking foot.
The speed difference between ball and foot. This is the only thing the ball 'feels' in the collision.
Moving the foot back with the ball as it arrives, so the speed difference shrinks and the ball stays close.
How heavy the foot acts in the collision. A tense leg acts heavier and throws the ball harder; a relaxed leg acts lighter and softer.
The roughly nine thousandths of a second the ball and foot are touching.
The grass brake: how many metres per second a rolling ball loses every second.
A ball released from a one-metre-high ramp must roll 4 to 8 metres (top-grade pitch) or 4 to 10 metres before it stops.
How fast the nearest defender is shrinking the gap to the ball.
Seconds until the nearest defender reaches the ball. Two metres at six metres per second is a third of a second.
The foot farther from the passer. Receiving on it opens your body and lets the touch travel across you, away from pressure.
Standing side-on so you can see the ball and the goal at the same time.

jargon_map.term: Directional first touch / receiving to redirect
jargon_map.plain_version: A first touch that sends the ball to where your next action starts, not to your own feet.

jargon_map.term: Touch into space / positive first touch
jargon_map.plain_version: A first touch that moves the ball about one to three metres away from the defender.
Literally 'take on and take along': receive and move the ball in one action.
Before the ball arrives, look for Ball, Opposition, Teammates, Space.
Cushion: soft surface gives with the ball. Wedge: sole traps the ball against the ground.
One player's turn on the ball. In top leagues it lasts about one second and two touches on average.
The quarter of a second between seeing something and starting to move.

claims.claim: Law 2: a size 5 match ball has a circumference of 68-70 cm, a mass of 410-450 g at kick-off and a pressure of 0.6-1.1 atmosphere.

FIFA Quality Pro size 5 balls must rebound 135-155 cm (FIFA Quality: 125-155 cm) when dropped from 2.00 m onto a metal plate. That is a coefficient of restitution of about 0.82-0.88 on a rigid surface.

Measured coefficient of restitution of two recent match balls (Uniforia, Al Rihla) on a rigid anvil with the FIFA method: 0.78-0.80 at 0.6 bar and 0.81-0.83 at 1.0 bar. Pressure is the dominant factor (about 4 percent).

In instep kicking, the ball-foot coefficient of restitution ranges from 0.463 to 0.681 and depends on the ball, the shoe, the ankle and the foot. Raising it from 0.5 to 0.65 would raise ball speed by about 10 percent (adult males, review).
Asai et al. (2002) reported a foot-ball COR of 0.50 at a foot speed of 18.6 m/s (as cited by Kapidzic et al. 2014).

Ball-to-foot speed ratios in instep kicks range from 1.06 to 1.65 (review). On a mechanical kicking leg a rigid ankle gave 1.16 and a non-rigid ankle 1.10, because rigidity increases the effective mass and cuts energy loss. A softer joint therefore sends the ball away slower.
In maximal instep kicks (11 adult players, 5000 Hz video) foot-ball contact lasted 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms, the ball deformed by 6.2 +/- 0.6 cm and peak ball reaction force reached 2926 +/- 509 N.

In submaximal side-foot kicks (8 university players) the ball/foot velocity ratio fell at 50 and 75 percent effort, which the authors attribute to players loosening ankle fixation towards impact. The same lever (ankle stiffness) that pros use to soften a pass softens a first touch.
claims.value: lower ball/foot ratio at lower effort

claims.claim: Maximal instep-kick ball speeds are 18-35 m/s in adults depending on skill, age and approach (review); 15-18-year-olds about 32 m/s; World Cup professionals 32-35 m/s.
Prepubescent boys (n = 31) kicking a stationary ball as hard as possible with the instep reached a mean maximal ball speed of 17.3 +/- 2.3 m/s (radar).
Maximal side-foot (pass) kicks in adults reach about 23.4 m/s versus 28.0 m/s for instep kicks (Levanon & Dapena 1998, as cited by Kapidzic et al. 2014).

In professional training (21 players, foot-mounted IMUs) a 'high-speed' ball release was defined as more than 15 m/s, and only about 8-18 of roughly 100-160 daily releases exceeded it. Most match-style passes therefore leave the foot slower than 15 m/s.

Typical ground-pass speeds: no primary tracking-data source with a mean pass speed was found. Working estimate for the script: youth (U12-U16) 5-10 m/s, adults 8-15 m/s, with hard driven passes 15-20 m/s. Inferred from maximal-kick data (17 m/s youth, 23 m/s adult side-foot) and the 15 m/s high-speed threshold above. Flag as estimate.

FIFA ball roll test: the ball is placed on a ramp so its centre is 1000 +/- 5 mm above the surface, released, and the roll distance is measured. The test ball must rebound 1.35 +/- 0.03 m on concrete from 2.0 m (COR 0.82).

FIFA Football Turf requirements (2024 Test Manual II): ball roll length 4.0-8.0 m for FIFA Quality Pro and 4.0-10.0 m for FIFA Quality; vertical ball rebound 0.60-0.85 m (Pro) and 0.60-1.00 m (Quality) from a 2 m drop. The Pro range is designed to replicate good natural grass.
FIFA 2-star (professional) turf limits were set to replicate good-quality natural grass; vertical ball rebound 0.60-0.85 m from a 2 m drop.

Derived: a ball rolling off the FIFA ramp leaves at about 3.6-3.7 m/s. Rolling 4 to 8 m (Quality Pro) means a deceleration of roughly 0.8-1.7 m/s^2; 10 m means about 0.7 m/s^2. Rule of thumb for the script: a rolling ball on a good pitch loses about 1 m/s every second. So a first touch that leaves the foot at 2 m/s rolls about 1.3-3 m and stops in about 2 s; at 5 m/s it rolls 8-18 m.

Derived rebound arithmetic (heavy-foot approximation, ball speed 10 m/s): a still stiff foot with e = 0.5 sends the ball back at about 5 m/s (12 m roll); a foot moving back at one-third of ball speed stops it dead (for e = 0.7 about 40 percent of ball speed is needed); a foot moving into the ball at 2 m/s sends it back at 8 m/s. Plain rule: the ball only bounces off the speed difference.
claims.value: dead stop at foot speed = e/(1+e) of ball speed = 33-41%

claims.claim: Youth sprint times (Slovak club players, standing start, photocells): U12 10 m 2.04 s and 30 m 5.28 s; U14 2.00 s and 5.05 s; U16 1.85 s and 4.43 s. That is about 4.9-5.4 m/s over the first 10 m and 6.2-7.8 m/s over 10-30 m.

claims.claim: Elite youth (116 boys aged 11-17, grouped by maturity, crouch start): 10 m split 2.38 s (2 years before growth spurt) to 2.16 s (3 years after); 30 m 5.51 s to 4.67 s; speed over the last 10 m rises from about 6.5 to 8.3 m/s.

In highly trained U14, U16 and U18 players, acceleration (10 m), maximum running speed (flying 20 m) and repeated sprints all improve with age; differences vanish when adjusted for biological maturity.
Professional adult players (n = 25, 25 years): 5 m in 1.04 s and 30 m in 4.22 s from a standing start, so about 7.9 m/s average over 5-30 m.

Bundesliga professionals reach maximum velocities above 9 m/s in matches; English Premier League sprints are defined as at least 7.0 m/s and 66 percent begin as rolling accelerations rather than from standing.
Most Premier League sprints start from a linear, forward-moving, rolling acceleration (66 percent) and are curved (86 percent).

Derived time-bubble table: at a closing speed of 5 m/s each metre is 0.20 s; at 6 m/s 0.17 s; at 8 m/s 0.12 s. Youth defenders at speed (about 6 m/s) give 0.17 s per metre; pros at speed (8-9 m/s) 0.11-0.12 s; from a standing start over the first 5-10 m everyone averages only about 4.5-5.5 m/s, so about 0.2 s per metre. Script rule: about a fifth of a second per metre.
French Ligue 1 (30 matches): mean individual possession lasted 1.1 +/- 0.1 s with 2.0 +/- 0.2 touches, covered 4.2 m, and players received the ball at 10.3 km/h (2.9 m/s), that is, on the move.

Bundesliga (60 matches, 69,667 intervals): a player's individual ball control interval averaged 1.2 +/- 1.0 s; 836 such intervals per match; central forwards shortest (0.9 s), goalkeepers longest (2.1 s).

Junior players (17.9 years, 4v4 games): the time between the first and second touch was shortest in the attacking third, longer in the middle and longest in the defensive third. Closer to goal, players need a faster first touch.

Simple visual reaction time in 1,469 adults averaged 231 ms (213 ms after correcting hardware delay); stimulus detection alone about 131 ms. Choice reactions in a game are slower. Supports the 'quarter of a second' teaser.

FA (England Football Learning, ages 12-16): 'Receive on their back foot so they open their body out to see the next player they're looking to pass to' and 'Scan for BOTS ... ball position, opposition players, teammates and space'.
FA (England Football Learning, ages 7-11): scan before receiving, learn a variety of receiving techniques, use the body to protect the ball.

FIFA Training Centre (Talent Coach Programme): 'Receiving players should offer for the ball at an angle to be able to receive on the back foot', 'receive on the back foot, facilitating playing forward more quickly', 'Players should scan before receiving', and use 'an outstretched arm to gauge the press'.

FIFA Training Centre (elite session 'Directing the ball with the first touch'): 'A receiving player's body orientation signals where they wish for the pass to be played and determines their ability to keep the ball under close control'; stationary players 'may not be able to generate the speed ... to turn quickly without losing the ball'.

claims.claim: US Youth Soccer Skills School manual, inside-of-foot ground ball: 'turn the toes of the receiving foot out so that the arch of the foot is facing the oncoming ball; extend the receiving foot slightly forward; watch the ball onto the receiving foot ... as the ball makes contact with the foot gently pull the leg backward to absorb the pace of the ball; keep the sole of the foot parallel with the ground'. Then teach 'receiving to redirect': inside of the foot across the body, outside of the foot to the outside, 180-degree turns. U8: inside and sole; U10: instep and outside.
claims.value: pull the leg back; redirect across the body

claims.claim: KNVB Assist lists 'aan- en meenemen' (receive and take along) as one of the core technical actions to train in every session, alongside dribbling, passing and shooting. No detailed KNVB receiving cues were retrievable (site is app-based).

Blind footballers keep their head turned toward the approaching ball throughout trapping, and sighted beginners who were told to follow the ball with their face made fewer trapping errors. Supports the cue 'watch the ball onto the foot'.

Gap: searches of Europe PMC and OpenAlex found no peer-reviewed biomechanics study of ground-ball reception (foot retraction speed, ankle stiffness during trapping) in sighted football. The cushioning numbers in this brief are derived from collision physics plus kicking-impact data, not from trapping measurements.

technique_cues: Look before it arrives: scan for BOTS (ball, opponents, teammates, space) while the pass is still travelling.
Arrive at an angle, side-on, so you can see the ball and the goal at once.
Take it on the back foot (the foot farther from the passer) and let the touch travel across your body, away from the defender.
Soft ankle, foot moving back: meet the ball with the foot slightly forward, then pull the leg back as it touches. The ball only bounces off the speed difference.
Sole parallel to the ground, toes turned out so the arch faces the ball (inside of foot).
Aim the touch at a spot one to three metres away, in the space you found in your scan. Not at your own feet.
Weight of touch: the ball should leave your foot at jogging pace, about two metres per second, so grass stops it in about two metres.
Receive on the move: a stationary player cannot turn quickly without losing the ball.
Watch the ball onto the foot for the last metre, then eyes up.
Use the outstretched arm to feel where the press is coming from while you receive.
Your body shape is a message: open it toward where you want the pass, and your teammate will pass to that foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Killing the ball dead under the feet as the default touch.
common_mistakes.consequence: Zero metres and zero time gained; the defender keeps closing at 5-8 m/s and you need an extra touch (and about half a second) to start again.
common_mistakes.fix: Let the foot give a little less than the dead-stop amount so the ball rolls one to three metres into the space you scanned.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stiff, locked leg or foot planted still (or worse, moving toward the ball).
common_mistakes.consequence: The ball keeps about half of its speed: a 10 m/s pass bounces away at about 5 m/s and rolls 8-12 m.
common_mistakes.fix: Relax the ankle and start the foot moving back with the ball before contact; about a third of the ball's speed stops it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Toe up, sole not parallel to the ground, or contact with the toe/heel edge.
common_mistakes.consequence: The ball pops up or squirts sideways; the touch direction is random.
common_mistakes.fix: Toes out, arch facing the ball, sole flat and just off the grass; watch the ball onto the foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Receiving square-on with the near foot.
common_mistakes.consequence: Your body faces the passer, your back is to the goal, and the touch goes toward the pressure.
common_mistakes.fix: Offer at an angle, half-turn, and take it on the back foot across the body.

common_mistakes.mistake: Head down from the moment the pass is played.
common_mistakes.consequence: You receive with no picture, so the first touch has nowhere to go.
common_mistakes.fix: Scan two or three times while the ball travels, then watch the ball for the last metre.

common_mistakes.mistake: Touch too heavy (ball leaves at 4-5 m/s).
common_mistakes.consequence: On a good pitch it rolls 8-18 m: you have passed it to nobody.
common_mistakes.fix: Practise the 'two-metre rule' against a wall: the ball must stop inside a two-metre gate.

common_mistakes.mistake: Standing still and waiting for the pass.
common_mistakes.consequence: A stationary player cannot turn quickly; pros receive while moving at about 3 m/s.
common_mistakes.fix: Check away, then come to the ball at an angle and receive on the move.

drills: Wall bounce meter (alone): pass at a wall from 5 m. First, receive with a stiff, still foot and mark how far the ball rolls away. Then receive with a giving foot. Aim for the ball to stop within one metre (dead-stop) and then within a two-metre gate (touch into space). Safety: use a solid wall with no windows or doors, away from roads; check the surface for stones and holes.

Speed-difference lab (alone): pass at the wall softly, medium and hard. Keep the same relaxed foot and notice that the rebound off your foot grows with pass speed. Then match your foot's backward speed to the pass so every rebound lands in the same spot. Safety: start soft; do not use a hard pass until the soft one is under control.

Back-foot gate (alone): put two cones 2 m apart, 3 m from the wall and at 45 degrees to it. Pass to the wall, receive the rebound on the back foot across your body and send the first touch through the gate, then pass again from the new spot. Switch sides every ten reps. Safety: warm up ankles and hips first; keep the cones low so you cannot trip.

Two-touch clock (alone): pass at the wall, first touch into space, second touch back to the wall. Count seconds per cycle; try to get near the pro rhythm of about one second and two touches. Stop when technique breaks down, not when tired. Safety: rest between sets.

Time bubble with a friend: friend passes, then chases the ball as soon as it leaves their foot. You must take one touch into space and pass back before they reach you. Move the friend 1 m closer each round and feel how much each metre is worth. Safety: no tackling; the chaser stops at arm's length.

Scan-and-call with a friend: friend passes; while the ball travels they hold up left or right hand. You must look, then take your first touch to the opposite side and call the hand you saw. Safety: keep the passing distance at 5-8 m so passes stay controllable.

Pressure-arm receive with a friend: friend stands behind you as a passive defender and taps a shoulder as the ball arrives. Receive side-on, feel the tap with your outstretched arm and take your touch away from that side. Safety: taps only, no pushing; agree the signal before you start.
Ball choice for U12: use a size 4 ball (350-390 g) if that is your age-group ball, so the rebound behaviour matches your matches.
animation_ideas: Speed-difference meter: a bar between the ball's arrow and Tavi's foot arrow. Stiff foot: full bar, ball springs off. Giving foot: bar shrinks to a third, ball settles. Same pass, three foot modes side by side.

Ultra slow-motion contact: nine milliseconds stretched to nine seconds; the ball squashes like a spring (up to 6 cm in a hard kick, a dimple for a pass) and pushes back only as hard as it was squashed.
The grass brake gauge: a rolling ball with a speedometer losing about 1 m/s every second; a 2 m/s touch dies in 2 m, a 5 m/s bounce keeps going past Chalk's line.
Time bubble ring: a ring around Tavi labelled in seconds, radius = distance / Chalk's speed. Each metre of first touch grows the ring by about a fifth of a second; a stopwatch ticks the gain.
Chalk's closing-speed comparison: a youth chalk defender (about 6 m/s) versus a pro chalk defender (about 8-9 m/s), both erased metre by metre as the ring shrinks.
Egg catch overlay: Tavi's foot path traced next to two hands catching an egg, same backward motion, same idea.
Heat map of first-touch landing spots: red for 'under the feet' and 'bounced away', green for a crescent one to three metres away from the defender's side.
Back-foot split screen: near foot square-on (view cone points back to Sam) versus back foot half-turn (view cone includes ball and goal).
The one-second, two-touch rhythm: a metronome over pro possessions, showing why touch one must already be the start of action two.
Body-shape message: Tavi opens the hips and a dotted 'pass here' arrow appears for Sam, showing that the first touch starts before the pass is even played.
The FIFA ramp cameo: a ball rolling off a one-metre ramp onto the night pitch and stopping between the 4 m and 8 m chalk marks, to introduce the grass brake number.
misconceptions: 'The ball bounces because my foot is hard.' It bounces because of the speed difference. A hard foot that is moving back with the ball gives a soft touch; a soft foot moving into the ball gives a hard bounce.
'Stop it dead first, then look.' A dead ball buys no time. The scan happens before the ball arrives, and the first touch already moves you into space.
'A harder pass always means a worse touch.' A faster pass needs a faster giving foot, not a different technique. The rule stays: match about a third of the ball speed to kill it.
'Good first touch means the ball never leaves your foot.' Pros receive on the move at about 3 m/s and their touch travels one to three metres. Glued-to-the-foot control is for tight spaces only.
'Fast players do not need a good touch.' Individual possessions in top leagues last about one second and two touches; the time is bought with the touch, not with legs.
'The sole trap is the basic first touch.' The wedge is one tool; the cushion with inside, outside or instep, moving the ball to a spot, is the everyday tool.
'A soft touch means slow, lazy feet.' The giving foot is a fast, timed movement backward; the leg moves as quickly as the ball demands.
'Metres do not matter, only speed.' On the pitch every metre of space is about a fifth of a second of defender time, which is roughly one reaction time.

'Youth passes are as fast as adult passes, so the numbers are the same.' Youth passes and youth defenders are both slower, so the time per metre is similar (about 0.15-0.25 s), but the absolute distances the ball rolls are shorter.

verdicts.claim: Law 2: size 5 ball 68-70 cm, 410-450 g, 0.6-1.1 atm
verdicts.note: IFAB Law 2.1 text matches: 68-70 cm, 410-450 g at the start of the match, 0.6-1.1 atmosphere (600-1,100 g/cm2) at sea level.

verdicts.claim: FIFA Quality Pro size 5 rebound 135-155 cm (Quality 125-155 cm) from 2.00 m onto a metal plate; COR about 0.82-0.88
verdicts.corrected_value: Pro 135-155 cm at 20 C (min 125 cm at 5 C); Quality and Basic 125-155 cm (min 115 cm at 5 C); COR 0.82-0.88 (Pro), 0.79-0.88 (Quality)
verdicts.note: FIFA Quality Programme for Footballs Test Manual v1.2 (Dec 2023), Test 03: guided free fall from 2.00 +/- 0.01 m (bottom of ball), impact speed 6.25 m/s, onto a metal anvil on a base of at least 1000 kg. Table 4.1 gives 135-155 / 125-155 / 125-155 cm for the three size-5 columns. The column labels are an image. The stricter tolerances in column 1 identify it as Quality Pro. Spread across the 3 balls max 10 cm.

verdicts.claim: Uniforia and Al Rihla COR 0.78-0.80 at 0.6 bar and 0.81-0.83 at 1.0 bar; pressure about 4 percent
verdicts.note: England et al. 2025, Ann Biomed Eng, 'Does Reduced Ball Inflation Pressure in Association Football Decrease Head Impact Kinematics?'. This is a heading-impact study. COR came from the ball characterisation (FIFA QP method, 3 impact locations, 5 repeats). Table 4: Uniforia 0.781-0.800 at 0.6 bar and 0.818-0.825 at 1.0 bar. Al Rihla 0.776-0.794 and 0.811-0.823. Pressure raised COR by 0.030-0.033, 'around 4%'. Impact location changed it by about 0.02. Say 'about 80 percent' rather than 'more than 80 percent'.

verdicts.claim: Foot-ball COR 0.463-0.681; raising it from 0.5 to 0.65 gives about 10 percent more ball speed
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis 2007, J Sports Sci Med (narrative review). Exact quotes match. The COR values come from adult male maximal kicks at foot speeds of 18-28 m/s. Nobody has measured COR at receiving speeds, so do not present 0.5 as a measured value for a first touch.

verdicts.claim: Asai et al. (2002) reported COR 0.50 at foot speed 18.6 m/s (as cited by Kapidzic 2014)
verdicts.corrected_value: Dorge et al. (2002), not Asai et al. (2002)
verdicts.note: Kapidzic et al. 2014 write: 'Dorge et al. (2002) reported that a high speed of the foot (18.6 m/s) and a high angular velocity (28.1 rad/s) led to a high coefficient of restitution (COR = 0.50)'. Dorge et al. 2002 (J Sports Sci, doi 10.1080/026404102753576062) did compute a foot-ball COR for preferred vs non-preferred leg in 7 skilled players. Kapidzic cite Asai et al. as 2005, a different paper.

verdicts.claim: Ball-to-foot ratios 1.06-1.65; mechanical leg rigid ankle 1.16 vs non-rigid 1.10 because of effective mass and energy loss
verdicts.note: Peacock & Ball 2018, J Biomech: rigid 1.16 +/- 0.02, non-rigid 1.10 +/- 0.01, p < 0.001, 4000 Hz, 10 trials per configuration. 'The rigid ankle was characterised by significantly greater effective mass and significantly less energy losses.' The 1.06-1.65 range is from Kellis & Katis 2007. The paper is about kicking, not receiving. The transfer to a first touch is the script's inference.

verdicts.claim: Maximal instep kicks: 11 players, 5000 Hz, contact 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms, deformation 6.2 +/- 0.6 cm, peak force 2926 +/- 509 N
verdicts.note: Shinkai, Nunome, Isokawa & Ikegami 2009, Med Sci Sports Exerc. All numbers match the abstract. Mean force was 1403 +/- 129 N. These are maximal kicks. Contact time for a slow cushioned touch is not measured and is probably a little longer.

verdicts.claim: Submaximal side-foot kicks: lower ball/foot ratio at 50 and 75 percent, attributed to looser ankle fixation
verdicts.note: Nunome, Inoue, Watanabe & Akima, Sports Biomech (online 2023, issue 2025). 8 male university players, 500 Hz. 'Significantly smaller ball/foot velocity ratios in the two submaximal conditions suggested ankle joint fixation was manipulated towards ball impact.' The second sentence of the claim (same lever softens a first touch) is the script's extrapolation, not the paper's.

verdicts.claim: Maximal instep ball speeds 18-35 m/s in adults; 15-18-year-olds about 32 m/s; World Cup pros 32-35 m/s
verdicts.note: Kellis & Katis 2007: 'range from 18 to 35 m/s', 32.1 m/s for 15-18-year-olds, 32-35 m/s at the 1990 World Cup. Older male data. Not representative of U12 or of passing.

verdicts.claim: Prepubescent boys (n = 31) maximal instep kick of a stationary ball: 17.3 +/- 2.3 m/s by radar
verdicts.note: Deniz & Kilci 2025, PeerJ. 'The mean value of the maximum ball speed was 17.3 +/- 2.3 m/s.' 31 boys aged 11-12, stationary ball, Bushnell radar gun, 11 m to a 2 x 2 m target. The ball is described as 'standard-sized (Lotto FB1000 4)' at 11 psi (0.76 bar). Ball size is not stated unambiguously and is probably size 4 for this age.

verdicts.claim: Adult side-foot max 23.4 m/s vs instep 28.0 m/s (Levanon & Dapena 1998 via Kapidzic 2014)
verdicts.note: Kapidzic et al. quote side-foot ball speed 23.4 +/- 1.7 m/s (foot 19.1 m/s) vs instep 28.0 +/- 2.1 m/s (foot 20.3 m/s).

verdicts.claim: Pro training IMUs (21 players): high-speed release > 15 m/s; about 8-18 of roughly 100-160 daily releases exceed it
verdicts.corrected_value: 12-18 high-speed releases out of 128-161 total per session (means by training day)
verdicts.note: Lewis et al. 2022, PLOS ONE. 21 EFL Championship players (25.5 y), PlayerMaker foot IMUs. Per-session means: total releases 127.6 (MD-4) to 161.1 (MD+1). High-speed (> 15 m/s) 12.1 to 17.6. Training only, no match data. The 15 m/s cutoff has no stated justification. 'Most match-style passes leave the foot slower than 15 m/s' is an inference from training counts.

verdicts.claim: Typical ground-pass speeds: youth 5-10 m/s, adults 8-15 m/s, driven 15-20 m/s (estimate)
verdicts.note: No match-tracking study with a mean pass speed was found (Europe PMC queries only, web search budget exhausted). One skill-test paper (Rodriguez-Giustiniani et al. 2022, Sci Med Football, 10 academy players aged 18) reports 4.2 m short passes at 11.1 and 7.9 m long passes at 12.2, printed as km/h but almost certainly m/s. Weak support for firm adult passes near 11-12 m/s. Keep the estimate flagged. For U12 a typical pass is probably 5-8 m/s, so the story's 10 m/s pass is an adult firm-pass figure.

verdicts.claim: FIFA ball roll test: centre of ball 1000 +/- 5 mm above surface; test ball rebounds 1.35 +/- 0.03 m on concrete from 2.0 m (COR 0.82)
verdicts.note: Turf-Tec booklet quoting the FIFA Football Turf Handbook (Oct 2015): 'the point below the center of the ball sitting on the ramp is 1000 +/- 5 mm above the test area'. Test ball: FIFA Quality Pro, adjusted to rebound 1.35 +/- 0.03 m on concrete from 2.0 m. sqrt(1.35/2.00) = 0.82. Roll distance is measured from first contact with the surface to rest. Vendor document, not FIFA itself.

verdicts.claim: FIFA Turf Test Manual II (2024): ball roll 4.0-8.0 m (Pro), 4.0-10.0 m (Quality); rebound 0.60-0.85 m (Pro), 0.60-1.00 m (Quality) from 2 m
verdicts.corrected_value: Quality: 4.0-10.0 m initial, 4.0-12.0 m after simulated wear and on retests
verdicts.note: Version June 2024. Table: vertical ball rebound 0.60-0.85 m (Pro) / 0.60-1.00 m (Quality). Ball roll 4.0-8.0 m (Pro) / 4.0-10.0 m (Quality, preconditioned) and 4.0-12.0 m after simulated wear. Introduction: football turf must 'replicate the playing characteristics of good-quality natural grass'. The 2 m drop is in the Test Methods manual, confirmed by the Turf-Tec booklet and Fleming 2015.

verdicts.claim: FIFA 2-star (professional) turf limits replicate good-quality natural grass; rebound 0.60-0.85 m from 2 m
verdicts.note: Fleming, Forrester & McLaren 2015: 'The FIFA 2* category is designated for professional use with the upper and lower limits for each test defined to replicate good quality natural grass.' Table: vertical ball rebound 0.60-1.00 m (1*), 0.60-0.85 m (2*). The paper is about infill decompaction. 2-star is the old name for Quality Pro.

verdicts.claim: Derived: ramp exit 3.6-3.7 m/s; deceleration 0.8-1.7 m/s2 (4-8 m), 0.7 m/s2 (10 m); rule about 1 m/s per second; 2 m/s touch rolls 1.3-3 m in about 2 s; 5 m/s rolls 8-18 m
verdicts.corrected_value: Exit speed about 3.2-3.4 m/s. Deceleration about 0.65-1.4 m/s2 for 4-8 m and about 0.5-0.6 m/s2 for 10 m. A 2 m/s touch rolls 1.4-4 m and stops in 1.4-4 s. A 5 m/s touch rolls 9-25 m.
verdicts.note: The 3.6-3.7 m/s figure ignores the rotational kinetic energy of a rolling shell and uses the full 1.0 m. The ball centre drops only about 0.89 m (1.00 m minus a 0.11 m radius). For a thin shell rolling without slip v = sqrt(2 g h / (1 + 2/3)) = 3.2 m/s at h = 0.89 m (3.4 m/s at h = 1.0 m), and lower if the ball rolls on rails. With a = v2/2d the FIFA Pro range gives 0.65-1.4 m/s2. 'About one metre per second each second' is still the right order of magnitude but sits in the upper half. The story's 'twelve metres' for a 5 m/s ball is a fair mid-range figure. 'Two metres in two seconds' is at the short end. Constant deceleration is an approximation and real grass varies with cut and moisture.

verdicts.claim: Derived rebound arithmetic (heavy foot, 10 m/s pass): still foot e = 0.5 returns 5 m/s; retreat at one-third stops it (e/(1+e) = 33-41 percent); foot into ball at 2 m/s returns 8 m/s
verdicts.corrected_value: Formula direction and arithmetic correct for an infinitely heavy foot. With a realistic effective foot mass of about 1.7-3 kg (4-7 ball masses) and e = 0.5-0.65, a still firm foot returns about 2-4 m/s (20-40 percent), and a dead stop needs a retreat of about 15-30 percent of ball speed.
verdicts.note: 1-D collision: v_out = e v_b - w(1+e) for a foot retreating at w, so dead stop at w = e v_b/(1+e). That is right for M >> m. Kicking data (ball/foot ratio about 1.2 at e about 0.5) imply an effective foot mass of about 1.7 kg, so the general form v_out = [(eM - m) v_b + (1+e) M u]/(M+m) gives 2 m/s for a still foot at M = 1.7 kg, e = 0.5, and about 4 m/s at M = 2.5 kg, e = 0.65. The COR of 0.46-0.68 comes from kicks at 18-28 m/s foot speed and is not measured at receiving speeds. Narrate 'about a third to a half of its speed' and 'pull back at roughly a quarter to a third of the ball speed'.

verdicts.claim: Slovak youth sprints: U12 10 m 2.04 s, 30 m 5.28 s; U14 2.00 / 5.05; U16 1.85 / 4.43; about 4.9-5.4 m/s over 10 m and 6.2-7.8 m/s over 10-30 m
verdicts.note: Bakalar et al. 2020, J Exerc Rehabil. 41 players from one Slovak academy (U12 n = 15, U14 n = 14, U16 n = 12). Standing start, dominant foot behind the line, Witty photocells, best of three. Times match. Derived speeds are correct (U12 6.2 m/s, U16 7.8 m/s over 10-30 m). Small single-club sample.

verdicts.claim: Elite youth (116 boys 11-17, maturity groups, crouch start): 10 m 2.38 to 2.16 s; 30 m 5.51 to 4.67 s; last 10 m speed about 6.5 to 8.3 m/s
verdicts.note: Zghal et al. 2025, Eur J Sport Sci. 116 elite boys in six groups PHV-2 to PHV+3, three-point crouch start, MySprint video splits. 10 m: 2.38 (PHV-2) to 2.16 s (PHV+3). 30 m: 5.51 to 4.67 s. The 20 m split was not extracted. The 25-30 m segment gives 6.4 m/s (PHV-2) to 8.5 m/s (PHV+3), consistent with the claim.

verdicts.claim: Highly trained U14, U16, U18: acceleration, max speed and repeated sprints improve with age; differences vanish when adjusted for maturity
verdicts.note: Mendez-Villanueva et al. 2011, J Sports Sci. 61 players (U14 n = 14, U16 n = 22, U18 n = 25). U18 > U16 > U14 (P < 0.001). 'All between-group differences disappeared after adjustment for age at peak height velocity.'

verdicts.claim: Professional adults (n = 25, 25 years): 5 m in 1.04 s, 30 m in 4.22 s, standing start, about 7.9 m/s over 5-30 m
verdicts.note: Boraczynski et al. 2020, J Hum Kinet. 25 players (25.1 +/- 4.56 y), T5m 1.04 +/- 0.03 s, T30m 4.22 +/- 0.11 s, static start, Witty photocells. 25 m in 3.18 s = 7.9 m/s. Title says professional, abstract says elite.

verdicts.claim: Bundesliga pros exceed 9 m/s; EPL sprints defined as >= 7.0 m/s and 66 percent begin as rolling accelerations
verdicts.corrected_value: Bundesliga peak 9.32 +/- 0.11 m/s (high-ranked teams). The EPL 7.0 m/s definition and 66 percent rolling starts come from Caldbeck & Dos'Santos 2022, not from Chmura et al. Chmura's own sprint threshold is 6.3 m/s.
verdicts.note: Chmura et al. 2022, J Hum Kinet, reports maximum speeds of 9.32 +/- 0.11 m/s per match and uses 6.3 m/s as the sprint threshold. It says nothing about EPL sprint definitions or rolling starts. Cite PLOS ONE 10.1371/journal.pone.0277326 for those.

verdicts.claim: Most EPL sprints start from a rolling acceleration (66 percent) and are curved (86 percent)
verdicts.note: Caldbeck & Dos'Santos 2022. Sprint = velocity >= 7.0 m/s. 66 percent rolling starts, 86 percent curvilinear. 901 sprints, 10 matches, one EPL team, 2017-18.

verdicts.claim: Time-bubble table: 0.20 s/m at 5 m/s, 0.17 at 6, 0.12 at 8; youth 0.17 s/m at speed; pros 0.11-0.12; standing start 4.5-5.5 m/s so about 0.2 s/m
verdicts.note: Arithmetic is correct (1/5, 1/6, 1/8 s). Standing-start first 10 m: U12 4.9 m/s, U16 5.4 m/s, pros about 4.8 m/s over 5 m. Youth 10-30 m 6.2-7.8 m/s, pro peak 9.3 m/s. Caveat: what matters is the defender's closing speed relative to the ball at the moment of the touch, and most real sprints start rolling. 'About a fifth of a second per metre' is a fair rule.

verdicts.claim: Ligue 1 (30 matches): possession 1.1 +/- 0.1 s, 2.0 +/- 0.2 touches, 4.2 m, received at 10.3 km/h (2.9 m/s)
verdicts.note: Carling 2010, J Sports Sci. 30 French League 1 matches, one team (n = 28). Distance per possession 4.2 +/- 0.7 m, speed at ball reception 10.3 +/- 0.9 km/h, duration 1.1 +/- 0.1 s, touches 2.0 +/- 0.2. Mean time in possession per match 53.4 s. The study analyses 'running with the ball' possessions of one professional club.

verdicts.claim: Bundesliga (60 matches, 69,667 intervals): individual ball control 1.2 +/- 1.0 s; 836 per match; forwards 0.9 s, keepers 2.1 s
verdicts.note: Link & Hoernig 2017. 69,667 IBA intervals including 53,354 IBC. '836 +/- 424 IBC intervals per match.' Table 4: IBC per interval, all positions 1.2 +/- 1.0 s, central forwards 0.9 +/- 0.6 s, goalkeepers 2.1 +/- 0.8 s. The '1:21 min' figure in the same table is accumulated time per player per match, not per interval.

verdicts.claim: Junior players (17.9 y, 4v4): time between first and second touch shortest in the attacking third, longest in the defensive third
verdicts.note: Rosten, Aune & Dalen 2025, J Hum Kinet. 12 male juniors (17.9 +/- 0.8 y), 4v4 plus goalkeepers on 20 x 30 m. Shortest first-to-second-touch interval in the offensive zone, then centre, then defensive. Mean 0.92-0.95 s, minimum about 0.35 s. 'Closer to goal players need a faster touch' is an interpretation of an association. Population is 18-year-old juniors, not U12 or pros.

verdicts.claim: Simple visual reaction time in 1,469 adults 231 ms (213 ms corrected); detection about 131 ms
verdicts.note: Woods et al. 2015. 1,469 subjects aged 18-65, mean SRT 231 ms, 213 ms after a 17.8 ms hardware correction, stimulus detection time 131 ms. Adult data. Children's simple reaction times are longer (not verified here). 'About a quarter of a second' is safe for adults.

verdicts.claim: FA (12-16): receive on the back foot to open the body; scan for BOTS
verdicts.note: Quotes match verbatim: 'receive on their back foot so they open their body out to see the next player they're looking to pass to' and 'scan for BOTS ... ball position, opposition players, teammates and space'.

verdicts.claim: FA (7-11): scan before receiving, variety of receiving techniques, use the body to protect the ball
verdicts.note: Page is for ages 7-11. Quotes: 'try to scan before receiving the ball', 'learn how to use a variety of receiving techniques', 'using their body to protect the ball'.

verdicts.claim: FIFA Training Centre (Talent Coach Programme): offer at an angle, receive on the back foot, scan before receiving, outstretched arm to gauge the press
verdicts.note: All four phrases appear on the page verbatim.

verdicts.claim: FIFA Training Centre (elite session): body orientation signals the pass and determines close control; stationary players may not generate speed to turn
verdicts.note: Quotes match. Full sentence: 'If players are stationary and wish to turn quickly, they may not be able to generate the speed or possesses the efficiency to do so without losing the ball.'

verdicts.claim: US Youth Soccer Skills School manual: toes out, arch facing ball, foot forward, watch the ball onto the foot, pull the leg backward, sole parallel; receiving to redirect; U8 inside and sole, U10 instep and outside
verdicts.note: 2017 Skills School Manual, pages 33-34. Quotes match verbatim. Redirect list: inside to outside, inside across the body, inside 180 degrees, outside to outside, outside across the body, outside 180 degrees, inside behind the standing leg. Age progression: 'U8 ... receiving ground balls with the inside & sole of the foot', 'U10 ... receiving ground balls with the instep & outside of foot'.

verdicts.claim: KNVB Assist lists 'aan- en meenemen' as a core technical action
verdicts.note: Page lists 'Dribbelen, passeren, aan- en meenemen, passen, schieten en de bal afpakken van de tegenstander'. No receiving cues, only four general questions (right position, right moment, right speed, right direction).

verdicts.claim: Blind footballers turn the head toward the ball while trapping; sighted beginners told to follow the ball with the face made fewer errors; supports 'watch the ball onto the foot'
verdicts.corrected_value: Two separate studies. Mieda & Kokubu 2020 (Sci Rep): blind footballers vs sighted non-athletes, larger downward head rotation and better trapping. Mieda & Kokubu 2024 (PLOS ONE, 10.1371/journal.pone.0313336): 20 sighted students trained while wearing an eye mask. The 'follow the ball with your face' group made fewer errors at near distances. The mechanism is sound localisation, not vision.
verdicts.note: The 2024 methods state: 'participants were instructed to cover their eyes with an eye mask when performing the task'. So the evidence is about orienting the head to hear the ball in blind football. It is weak, indirect support for a visual 'watch the ball onto the foot' cue. Do not present it as evidence for that cue.

verdicts.claim: Gap: no peer-reviewed biomechanics study of ground-ball reception in sighted football found
verdicts.note: The given query returns 14 hits, none on sighted trapping biomechanics. A broader Europe PMC query (ball reception OR first touch OR ball control, kinematic OR biomechanic) also showed no such study in the top 25 of 301 hits. Not exhaustive: SPORTDiscus and Japanese-language journals were not searched. Keep the cushioning numbers labelled as derived.

verdicts.claim: UEFA coaching pages on receiving could not be retrieved
verdicts.note: Not retrieved in this session either (web search budget exhausted). The FIFA Training Centre pages stand as the confederation-level source.

mechanism_errors: 'A ball that hits a still, firm foot comes back with roughly half of its speed' is an upper bound from the infinitely-heavy-foot model. Kicking data imply an effective foot mass of about 1.7-3 kg (4-7 ball masses). With that, a still firm foot returns about 20-40 percent of the pass speed (2-4 m/s for a 10 m/s pass). Say 'a third to a half'.

'If the foot moves back at about a third of the ball's speed the ball just stops' follows from e/(1+e) with an infinitely heavy foot. With finite effective mass the dead-stop retreat is about 15-30 percent of ball speed. Say 'roughly a quarter to a third' or 'a few metres per second'.

The COR of 0.46-0.68 was measured in maximal kicks at 18-28 m/s foot speed. Nobody has measured foot-ball COR at receiving speeds (about 5-10 m/s relative). The ball alone gives 0.78-0.88 at 6.25 m/s on steel. The foot's real value for a first touch is unknown.

'Nine thousandths of a second' comes from maximal instep kicks (Shinkai 2009). Contact time for a slow cushioned touch has not been measured and is probably a little longer. Say 'about a hundredth of a second'.
'Dropped onto a steel plate it keeps more than 80 percent of its speed': measured 0.78-0.83 for Uniforia and Al Rihla, required 0.82-0.88 for FIFA Quality Pro. Say 'about 80 percent'.

Ramp exit speed is about 3.2-3.4 m/s, not 3.6-3.7 m/s. The derivation ignored the rotational kinetic energy of the shell and used a 1.0 m drop for the ball centre (it is about 0.89 m). Grass deceleration on FIFA-Pro-grade surfaces is then about 0.65-1.4 m/s2 for a 4-8 m roll and 0.5-0.6 m/s2 for 10 m. 'About one metre per second each second' is the upper half of the range.
