A 2 m/s touch rolls 1.4-4 m (not 1.3-3 m). A 5 m/s ball rolls 9-25 m. 'Twelve metres' is an acceptable mid-range figure.

Pro numbers are mixed into a youth scene. A 10 m/s pass is an adult firm pass (adult side-foot maximum 23.4 m/s, pro high-speed threshold 15 m/s). U12 passes are probably 5-8 m/s (prepubescent maximal instep kick 17.3 m/s). Receiving on the move at 2.9 m/s, 1.1 s and 2 touches per possession, and 4.2 m per possession are Ligue 1 professionals. The 0.9 s between touches is 18-year-old juniors in 4v4. Name the population in the narration.
'Their touch travels one to three metres' is inferred from 4.2 m per possession divided over about two touches in Ligue 1 pros. First-touch distance has not been measured directly.

The claim brief attributes the EPL sprint definition (>= 7.0 m/s) and the 66 percent rolling starts to the Bundesliga paper (Chmura 2022). They come from Caldbeck & Dos'Santos 2022. Chmura's own sprint threshold is 6.3 m/s.
The 'COR 0.50 at 18.6 m/s' figure is Dorge et al. 2002 as cited by Kapidzic 2014, not Asai et al. 2002.
The match-ball COR data (0.78-0.83) come from a heading-impact study (England et al. 2025) whose ball characterisation used the FIFA drop method. Cite it as such.

The blind-football evidence does not support 'watch the ball onto the foot' as a visual cue. Both groups in the 2024 training study wore eye masks. The effect is about turning the head to localise the ball by sound.

'A defender who is already running closes about five to eight metres every second' is right for youth-to-pro running speeds, but the time a touch buys depends on the defender's speed relative to the ball at that moment. Most match sprints start rolling. 'About a fifth of a second per metre' (standing-start speed) remains a fair rule for both youth and pros.
The 0.21-0.23 s simple reaction time is adult data (18-65 y). Youth reaction times are longer (not verified here). Say 'about a quarter of a second for an adult'.
The rebound story is right in direction: the ball rebounds off the speed difference, a retreating foot lowers the rebound, a foot moving into the ball raises it. Only the magnitudes need softening.
safe_numbers_for_narration: Law 2 (all levels): a size 5 ball is 68-70 cm around, weighs 410-450 g at kick-off and is inflated to 0.6-1.1 atmosphere.

FIFA Quality Pro size 5 balls must bounce back 135-155 cm when dropped 2 m onto a metal plate, so the ball keeps about 82-88 percent of its speed. Two recent tournament balls (Uniforia, Al Rihla) measured 0.78-0.83 by the same method.
In maximal instep kicks by 11 adult players, foot and ball touch for 9 ms, the ball squashes by 6.2 cm and the peak force is about 2,900 N.
On a mechanical kicking leg, a rigid ankle sends the ball off at 1.16 times foot speed, a loose ankle at 1.10 times. A stiffer joint gives a harder hit (adult kicking data).
Adults' maximal instep kicks reach 18-35 m/s. Adult side-foot (pass-style) maximal kicks reach about 23 m/s. Boys aged 11-12 (31 players) kicked a stationary ball at 17.3 m/s on average.
In professional training (21 EFL Championship players, foot sensors), a player releases the ball 128-161 times per session and only 12-18 of those leave the foot faster than 15 m/s.
FIFA Quality Pro turf, built to mimic good natural grass, must let a ball released from a 1 m ramp roll 4-8 m, and must bounce a ball 0.60-0.85 m from a 2 m drop.
Youth academy sprints (Slovak club, standing start): U12 run 30 m in 5.28 s and U16 in 4.43 s. Over 10-30 m that is about 6.2 m/s for U12 and 7.8 m/s for U16.
Elite youth boys: 30 m time improves from 5.51 s two years before the growth spurt to 4.67 s three years after it (116 players, crouch start).
From a standing start everyone covers the first 10 m at about 5 m/s: U12 4.9 m/s, U16 5.4 m/s, professional adults (5 m in 1.04 s) about 4.8 m/s. So about a fifth of a second per metre.

Professional adults (25 players): 30 m in 4.22 s. Bundesliga match peak speeds about 9.3 m/s. In the Premier League a sprint is 7 m/s or more, 66 percent start from a rolling run and 86 percent are curved.
Ligue 1 professionals (30 matches, one club): each possession lasts 1.1 s, uses 2.0 touches, covers 4.2 m, and the player receives the ball while moving at 2.9 m/s (10.3 km/h).
Bundesliga professionals (60 matches): a spell of individual ball control lasts 1.2 s on average, 836 per match. Central forwards 0.9 s, goalkeepers 2.1 s.
Junior players (age 18, 4v4 games): about 0.9 s between the first and second touch, shortest near the opponent's goal.
Adult simple visual reaction time is about 0.21-0.23 s (1,469 people).
Time per metre at a given closing speed: 0.20 s at 5 m/s, 0.17 s at 6 m/s (youth at speed), 0.12 s at 8 m/s (pros at speed).

FA (ages 12-16): receive on the back foot to open the body, and scan for BOTS (ball, opposition, teammates, space). FA (ages 7-11): scan before receiving, learn several receiving techniques, protect the ball with the body.

FIFA Training Centre: offer at an angle, receive on the back foot to play forward faster, scan before receiving, use an outstretched arm to feel the press. Body orientation signals where the pass should go.

US Youth Soccer (U8-U10): toes out so the arch faces the ball, foot slightly forward, watch the ball onto the foot, gently pull the leg back to absorb the pace, keep the sole parallel to the ground, then learn to redirect with inside and outside of the foot. U8 learns inside and sole, U10 adds instep and outside.

research.topic: SHAPE + REACTION: half-turn / open body and back foot, plus the vision, reaction-time and body-feint facts behind them (for U12-U16 explainer "Why the Best Players Look Slow", chapter 3 and bonus teaser)
research.one_line_hook: Your eyes see half a circle but read only a thumbnail, so the player who stands side-on sees the ball and the goal at once, and skips the half-second turn that gets everyone else caught.
research.mechanism_story:
Your eyes are wide but shallow. Together, the two eyes cover about 214 degrees from side to side. But sharp detail lives in one tiny spot in the middle, about the size of your thumbnail at arm's length. Two degrees away from that spot, detail is already half as good. Thirty degrees out, it is one sixteenth. The edges of your vision cannot read a shirt number. But they are good at one job: they catch movement. That is a built-in alarm for a defender who runs in from the side.

Now put Tavi on the pitch. Sam has the ball on the left. The goal is ahead. If Tavi turns square to face Sam, the goal sits far out to his side. The space behind him is fully out of view. His alarm covers the passer and nothing else. Chalk can arrive and Tavi never sees him. Now Tavi stands side-on, half turned. His chest points between Sam and the goal. The ball is about 45 degrees on one side. The goal is about 45 degrees on the other. Both sit inside his vision. One quick head turn puts the sharp spot on either one. In real matches, one scan takes elite players about four tenths of a second.

Body shape also saves time with the feet. Tavi receives on the back foot, the foot farther from Sam. The ball rolls across his body, and he already faces forward. No turn is needed. Compare that with a player who receives square and then spins 180 degrees with the ball. In tests with 11 to 15 year old players, a full turn cost about 0.6 seconds more than a straight run. Even a 90 degree turn cost about half a second. A defender who is already running covers about three metres in that time. The half turn does not make Tavi faster. It deletes a step that the other player still has to do.

The last piece is reaction time. To see one expected signal and move, a person needs about a quarter of a second. With a choice between options, it takes about half a second. Players aged 10 to 16 are a little slower than adults. A feint uses that delay. In one study a fake made players about half a second slower to reach the right place. Beginners guessed the wrong way about four times in ten. But the smart part is which body parts lie. Shoulders, head and the outside foot can fake. The hips and the body's weight tell the truth, and expert defenders wait and watch those.
plain_metaphors: Your vision is a very wide security camera with only one tiny high-definition pixel in the middle. Everything else is blurry motion detection.
The edge of your eye is a motion alarm, not a reading lamp. It tells you something moved, not who it is.
The half-turn is standing in a doorway: you can see both rooms without walking into either.
Receiving square to the passer is driving while staring into the rear-view mirror. The road ahead is a surprise.
A 180-degree turn with the ball is a U-turn in a car: brake, swing round, accelerate again. Side-on, you are already on the on-ramp.
Receiving on the back foot is a train passing through a station: the ball rolls through you and out the far side, and you are already facing the exit.
Reaction time is the lag on a video call. The event happened; the picture arrives a moment later. A feint sends a fake picture first.
Hips are the honest witness. Shoulders and head are the storytellers.
The time bubble: every scan you do before the ball arrives inflates the bubble. Every blind turn pops it.
More doors, slower choice: a feint adds a fake door, so the defender's brain has to think one door longer.

jargon_map.plain_version: Stand with your chest pointing between the ball and the goal, not straight at the passer, so you can see both.
The foot farther from the passer. Receiving with it lets the ball roll across your body so you already face forward.
The foot nearest the passer. Receiving with it stops the ball in front of you while you still face the passer.
Let the ball travel past your near foot and take it with the far foot, so your first touch points forward.
Chest facing the passer, back to the goal. You see the ball but not the space you want to play into.
A quick look away from the ball to see teammates, defenders and space before the ball arrives.
The blurry outer part of what you see. Bad at detail, good at spotting movement.
The tiny sharp spot in the middle of your sight, about the size of a thumbnail at arm's length.
The whole width you can see without moving your eyes or head, about 214 degrees side to side.
A fast eye jump from one spot to another. It takes a fraction of a second, and you see almost nothing during the jump.
Parking your eyes on a spot in between things so your side vision can watch several players at once.
How long it takes to react when you know exactly what signal is coming and what to do. About a quarter of a second.
How long it takes when you must first work out which of several things happened. About half a second.
The more options there are, the longer it takes to choose. Feints add fake options.
A move that shows the defender a false direction so they start moving the wrong way.
The balance point of your body, roughly behind your belly button. Where it goes, you go.
Body parts that must move where you are really going (hips, balance point) versus parts that can lie (shoulders, head, outside foot).
How much longer a run with a turn takes than the same distance run straight. It is the price of the turn.
A fitness test: run 5 metres, turn 180 degrees, run 5 metres back. It measures how fast you can turn.
How long your foot stays on the ground during a step. Sharp turns need long, heavy steps to brake.
The second-last step before a turn. Good turners do most of their braking there.
Standing where the defender cannot see you, usually behind their shoulder.
Swinging your foot around the ball without touching it to fake a direction.
Changing direction in response to something you see, like an opponent, rather than a planned route.

claims.claim: The human binocular visual field spans about 214 degrees horizontally; the temporal (outer) side of each eye reaches about 107 degrees.
claims.value: ~214 degrees horizontal diameter; 107 degrees temporal per eye

claims.claim: One eye sees about 60 degrees toward the nose and about 107 degrees away from the nose (Traquair perimetry).
Sharp detail is confined to the fovea: the foveola is about 1 degree across and the fovea about 5 degrees.
Visual acuity falls to half the foveal value by about 2 degrees off centre and to about one-sixteenth at 30 degrees (E2 for letter acuity about 2.3 degrees).
claims.value: half at 2 degrees; 1/16 at 30 degrees; E2 = 2.3 degrees

claims.claim: Peripheral vision is relatively good at detecting motion and flicker (magnocellular pathway); the periphery is specialised for temporal sensitivity, and simple reaction time rises about 1.66 ms per degree of eccentricity.
In sport, players often anchor gaze in free space between information sources and use peripheral vision to monitor several players at once ('gaze anchor' / 'visual pivot').

Vater, Williams and Hossner (2020) review the role of visual pivots and gaze anchors in sport (peripheral vision used for monitoring and motion detection). Full text was not retrievable in this session; DOI confirmed via Crossref.
A saccade (eye jump) lasts about 20 to 200 ms depending on size, normal saccade latency is about 200 ms, and gaze shifts larger than about 20 degrees also recruit a head movement.
claims.value: 20-200 ms duration; ~200 ms latency; >20 degrees needs head

claims.claim: In real 11v11 elite matches, one scan (head turn away from the ball) lasts on average 0.40 s (median 0.34 s); 90% of scans lasted 0.02-0.66 s; only 2.3% of scans contained a stable fixation, and those scans lasted about 0.97 s. Population: 4 Norwegian top-division central midfielders aged 17-23.
claims.value: mean 0.3965 s; median 0.34 s; 2.3% with fixations (0.97 s)

claims.claim: English Premier League players scanned 0.44 times per second before receiving; more scanning was associated with a higher probability of completing the pass (small effect, coefficient 0.13); players scanned least under tight pressure (0-1 m) and least before dribbling or shooting compared with passing. Population: 27 pros, 9,574 possessions.
claims.value: 0.44 scans/s; small positive effect on completion

claims.claim: Semi-elite players (16-30 y) turned their heads 1.44 times per second in the last second before receiving; players who explored more were more likely to turn with the ball, pass forward, and play to the side opposite to where the ball came from.
claims.value: 1.44 head turns/s in final second; 0.95/s over 10 s

claims.claim: Competitive-elite youth players (mean 16.25 y) explored most when in possession and in the back third, and least during transitions and in the middle third.

A scanning training programme (4v4 game formats and passing exercises that reward recognising visual cues) raised scanning in U19 female players from 0.88 to 1.44 scans per game situation, with gains kept after 3 weeks; elite players improved more than grassroots.
Among 8-10 year old players doing a passing test with eye tracking, the lower-performing group looked more at the ball while handling it; gaze strategies develop alongside technical skill.

No study was found that directly measures how much dribbling speed drops when a player looks up versus at the ball. 'Head up' is supported indirectly: better young players look at the ball less, pros scan less while dribbling than before passing, and elite U12-U16 players' response time to visual targets while passing improves about 30 ms per year. Treat 'head up costs speed' or 'head up is free' as unmeasured.

Elite U12 players (11.6 y) needed about 1100 ms to react to a visual target and pass to it; U15/U16 players about 1027 ms; response time improved about 30 ms per year of age, passing speed 2.3 km/h per year.
Adult simple visual reaction time (button press) is about 213-220 ms after correcting for hardware delay; it slows about 0.5 ms per year of adult age. Population: 1,469 adults 18-65.
Adult choice reaction time in a visual choice task was about 476 ms in the youngest adult group (mean 550 ms across 18-65), so choosing adds roughly 300 ms over a simple reaction.

In 38,778 people aged 10-18 doing a computer battery, simple reaction time (Detection task) fell from about 363 ms at age 10 to about 324 ms at 14-16 (log10 2.56 -> 2.51), and choice reaction time (Identification task) from about 575 ms at 10 to about 468 ms at 16 (log10 2.76 -> 2.67); speed reached adult level around 17-18. Values converted from the paper's log10 means; task includes a key press so they run higher than lab minimums.
Hick's law: decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices (Hick 1952, Hyman 1953).

World Athletics Technical Rules (Rule 16, The Start): a certified Start Information System flags a possible false start 'when the reaction time is less than 0.100 second' (Book C, C2.1, false-start section; Rules 16.7 and 16.8 cover false starts).

The 0.1 s threshold is a convention, not a hard human limit: in instrumented sprint starts, 20% of starts in two conditions were under 100 ms, the neuromuscular component can be under 85 ms and EMG latencies under 60 ms.
claims.value: <100 ms in 20% of starts; <85 ms possible

claims.claim: Wikipedia summary of the false-start rule and the physiological rationale (brain cannot process the gun in under 0.10 s), with citations to sprinters occasionally reacting in 0.08 s.

Adolescent male soccer players: a 505 test (5 m out, 180-degree turn, 5 m back) took 2.63 s at age 11.5 (pre-PHV), 2.55 s at 13.0 (circa-PHV) and 2.38 s at 15.4 (post-PHV), versus 10 m sprints of 2.06, 1.89 and 1.77 s; the change-of-direction deficit (turn cost) was 0.56, 0.66 and 0.61 s.
claims.value: 180-degree turn costs ~0.56-0.66 s vs straight run (ages 11-15)

claims.claim: Youth soccer U15-U18 (14.4-17.3 y): even a 90-degree turn in a 5 m + 5 m course cost 0.45-0.57 s more than a 10 m sprint (COD deficit), with total times 2.23-2.39 s versus 1.75-1.83 s straight.

Sharper change-of-direction angles need lower approach speed, longer braking distance, longer ground contact times and greater braking forces in the penultimate and final steps (angle-velocity trade-off); 180-degree turns are multi-step actions.
Faster 180-degree turners (modified 505) have shorter final ground contact times, lower vertical impact forces and do more of their braking on the penultimate step.
The COD deficit (505 time minus sprint time) isolates turning ability from straight speed (Nimphius et al. 2016).

In a soccer-player biomechanics study, 88% of participants exceeded ACL injury-risk thresholds during 180-degree tasks versus 19% at 45 degrees, so sharp turns should be taught with bent knees and progressive loading.

A feint in a life-size video reactive-agility test made Australian footballers 34% slower (about 509 ms longer agility time); movement time rose 197 ms in lower-standard players but only 62 ms in higher-standard players.
claims.value: +509 ms total; +197 ms vs +62 ms movement time

claims.claim: In a virtual-reality rugby side-step, novice defenders moved the wrong way 41.9% of the time versus 14.2% for experts; novices started moving earlier (about 193 ms) than experts (about 268 ms), who waited for honest information. Honest cues: centre-of-mass displacement and lower-trunk yaw. Deceptive cues: out-foot placement, head and upper-trunk yaw.
Skilled rugby attackers fool defenders by exaggerating head and upper-trunk movement while minimising centre-of-mass and lower-trunk movement ('balancing deceit and disguise').

A basketball head fake slows the defender's response by about 56 ms in dynamic video (6 ms with static pictures); experts resist deception better but are not immune (review of deceptive actions in sport).

For soccer step-overs, viewers read normal moves correctly 88.6% of the time but deceptive moves only 32.2%; lower-skilled players were worse than chance until the foot touched the ball (0 ms), higher-skilled players only until 80 ms before contact.
claims.value: 88.6% vs 32.2%; LS fooled to 0 ms, HS to -80 ms

claims.claim: In step-over judgements, upper-body information matters early and lower-body (hips down) information dominates later; low-skilled players are biased toward believing a move is genuine.

A single feint 'buys' roughly a quarter to half a second: defender simple reaction about 0.2-0.27 s (Woods; Brault initiation times) plus the extra 0.06-0.2 s of movement time and up to 0.5 s of total agility time a feint adds (Henry). This range is a synthesis across studies, not one measured number.

England Football Learning frames receiving around six core capabilities (scanning, timing, movement, positioning, deception, technique) and tells receivers to 'create a good angle to receive the pass' and 'get in position to play forward', use the blindside of the defender, and practise in 2v2/3v3 small-sided games.

England Football Learning on preparing before the ball arrives: see the path of the ball and the defender, see teammates' movement, see the space you want to use, move to create a good angle, move into a position to play forward, at the right time.

England Football Learning on turning: eight turn types (one-touch, no-touch, stop turn, inside hook, outside hook, drag back, stepover, Cruyff); for younger players use gates with some blocked off to force turns; add opposition as players mature.

England Football Learning receiving-session design uses the STEP framework: flat markers for 'safe zones' where players receive unopposed before defenders enter, weaker-foot receive-and-play-forward counts double, progress from pairs to 2v2/3v3/4v4.

The literal cues 'receive on the half-turn', 'on the back foot' and 'receive across your body' are standard UK/US coach-education language, but no FA, US Youth Soccer or US Soccer page containing these exact words could be retrieved in this session (US sites are JavaScript apps). Treat the wording as coaching convention rather than a sourced quote.
KNVB Rinus is the Dutch FA's free coaching platform with exercises and training plans by age; specific receiving/turning exercise pages could not be fetched (interactive catalogue).
Elite midfielders in match play use many short fixations (2,832 fixations analysed) and lengthen fixations when several information sources are present; fixations are shorter than in lab studies.
Peripheral vision in real-world tasks is used to monitor the environment and to relate one's own body to objects (systematic review of 60 papers).
More creative skilled players use a broader attentional focus with more, shorter fixations toward informative locations and detect threatening teammates earlier.

technique_cues: Chest to the pitch, not to the passer: point your belly button between the ball and the goal.
Side-on: one shoulder to the ball, one shoulder to the goal. Both are in your picture.
Last look as the ball leaves their foot: scan while the ball travels, then eyes back for the touch.
Back foot first: let the ball run across you and take it with the far foot.
First touch goes where you already looked, forward or into space, never back toward the passer.
Head up between touches. Keep the ball in the bottom corner of your eye, not in the middle.
Park your eyes in the gap between two players and let your side vision watch both.
Do the braking early: for any turn, slow down on the step before the plant, knees bent.
Attacking feint: big shoulders, quiet hips. Sell it with head, shoulders and outside foot, keep your balance point over your feet.
Defending a feint: watch the hips and the ball, ignore the shoulders. Wait a beat, then go.

common_mistakes.mistake: Receiving square to the passer with a closed body (chest to the ball, back to the goal).
common_mistakes.consequence: The goal side and the defender behind are outside a 214-degree field, so you receive blind. You then need a 180-degree turn with the ball, which costs 11-15 year olds about 0.6 s. A running defender covers about 3 m in that time.
common_mistakes.fix: Arrive side-on before the pass. Chest points between the ball and the goal. Take the ball on the back foot so no turn is needed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Taking the ball with the front foot (the foot nearest the passer).
common_mistakes.consequence: The ball stops in front of you while you still face the passer. Your next touch must go sideways or back.
common_mistakes.fix: Let the ball roll past the near foot and take it with the far foot. Cue: 'let it run across you'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ball-watching while the pass travels.
common_mistakes.consequence: Your picture is out of date by the time the ball arrives. Pressure and options have changed. Pros scan about 0.44 times per second before receiving; scanning less is linked to fewer completed forward passes.
common_mistakes.fix: Scan as the ball leaves the passer's foot. One 0.4 s head turn is enough. Then eyes back for the touch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Scanning too early or scanning without moving.
common_mistakes.consequence: The look is wasted. The scene changes in the last second, and a good angle needs feet as well as eyes.
common_mistakes.fix: Take the last look in the final second before the ball arrives and adjust your body angle while you look.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dribbling with the head down.
common_mistakes.consequence: The motion alarm of peripheral vision is pointed at the grass. Younger, weaker performers look at the ball more, and players scan less while dribbling than before passing.
common_mistakes.fix: Push the ball a touch farther, lift your eyes between touches and use the bottom of your vision to track the ball.

common_mistakes.mistake: Turning blind into pressure after no scan.
common_mistakes.consequence: You turn into the defender you never saw and lose the ball. Players who explore more before receiving turn more successfully and play forward more.
common_mistakes.fix: No look, no turn. Play back or sideways if you have not scanned.

common_mistakes.mistake: Faking with the whole body (moving the balance point).
common_mistakes.consequence: The centre of mass is the honest signal. If it goes with the fake, you cannot go the other way quickly and skilled defenders read it.
common_mistakes.fix: Exaggerate head, shoulders and outside foot; keep the hips and balance point centred over your feet.

common_mistakes.mistake: Defending: reacting to the shoulders as soon as they move.
common_mistakes.consequence: Novice defenders went the wrong way 42% of the time versus 14% for experts. Committing early gives the attacker a free half second.
common_mistakes.fix: Stay on the balls of your feet, watch the hips and the ball, wait about a quarter of a second longer than feels natural.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sharp 180-degree turns done upright with a stiff plant leg.
common_mistakes.consequence: Long ground contact, slow exit, and high knee load (most players exceed ACL-risk thresholds on 180-degree tasks).
common_mistakes.fix: Brake on the step before the plant, lower the hips, bend the knee and keep it over the toes, then push out low.

drills: Three-gate receiving (needs one friend). Set three flat-marker gates 5 m behind you (left, middle, right). Friend passes from 10 m and calls a gate as the ball leaves their foot. Scan for the call while the ball travels, receive side-on on the back foot, and take one touch through the named gate. 10 reps each side, then swap. Safety: use flat markers not tall cones, keep the running lane clear, start at walking pass speed.

Half-turn wall drill (alone). Stand side-on to a wall or rebounder, 3-4 m away. Pass with the near foot, let the rebound come across your body and take it with the far foot facing away from the wall, then dribble 3 m out and repeat. Count how many touches you need to face away; aim for one. Safety: choose a wall with no windows or traffic behind you, and check the surface is not slippery.

Colour-call scan (needs one friend). Friend stands 8-10 m away and passes; as the ball travels they hold up 1-5 fingers or a coloured bib behind their back position or to one side. You must call the number or colour before your first touch. Miss the call, restart. Based on drills that reward recognising visual cues, which raised scanning from 0.88 to 1.44 scans per situation in U19 players. Safety: none beyond space to move.

Square versus side-on race (needs one friend). Friend passes from 10 m then chases you as 'Chalk'. Round 1: receive square to the passer, turn 180 degrees and dribble through a gate 5 m behind you. Round 2: receive side-on on the back foot and go. Time both with a phone stopwatch and feel the half-second difference. Swap roles. Safety: shadow chase only, no slide or standing tackles, and 2 m gap at the start.

Measure your own turn cost (alone, phone stopwatch or a friend timing). Mark 5 m. Run 5 m out, turn 180 degrees, run 5 m back (505-style). Then run 10 m straight from the same start. The difference is your turn cost; 11-15 year olds average 0.56-0.66 s. Do 3 of each. Safety: warm up first, non-slip surface, brake on the step before the turn with a bent knee, stop if a knee or ankle hurts.

Honest-hips feint game (needs one friend). Face each other 2 m apart, one ball. Attacker tries to get past on either side using shoulder, head or step-over fakes. Defender may only look at the attacker's hips and the ball and must not move until the ball moves. Count how many times the defender is sent the wrong way in 10 goes, then swap. Safety: no contact, keep the 2 m gap, flat shoes on grass or turf.

Head-up dribble with finger flashes (needs one friend). Dribble through a 10 m slalom of flat markers while your friend, standing at the end, flashes fingers every 2 seconds. Call each number. Then repeat with your friend moving around the slalom so you must use side vision. Safety: clear area, markers flat, slow the pace before the count is right.

Blindside arrival (needs one friend as passer, or a wall). Place a cone as an imaginary defender. Start behind the cone, move to the far side of it (out of its 'sight'), receive side-on across your body and play forward in one touch. Based on England Football's 'blindside' and 'position to play forward' coaching points. Safety: flat cones, walk it first.
animation_ideas: Top-down 'vision cone' on Tavi: a 214-degree wedge shaded blurry blue, with a tiny sharp yellow pixel in the middle. As he rotates from square-on to side-on, Chalk walks from the black zone behind him into the blue motion zone and starts to 'ping' like radar.
Acuity fade: a heat-map that is bright at 0 degrees, half as bright at 2 degrees and nearly dark at 30 degrees. Overlay a shirt number that stays readable only inside the yellow dot.

Split-screen stopwatch: left, a square receiver turns 180 degrees (timer runs to 0.6 s while Chalk closes 3 m and the time bubble shrinks); right, side-on Tavi is already gone and his bubble stays the same size.
Back-foot train: the ball drawn as a train rolling through Tavi's 'station'. Front-foot version stops the train at the entrance with Tavi facing the wrong platform.
Scan clock: a small dial that ticks 0.4 s each time Tavi's head turns; the final tick fires exactly as the ball leaves Sam's foot.
Reaction ladder: bars for 0.1 s (false-start line, 'the rulebook says nobody is faster'), 0.2-0.25 s (simple reaction), 0.5 s (choice), then a feint bar that adds another 0.5 s in red.

Feint X-ray: Tavi's skeleton with shoulders and head glowing 'liar red' and the pelvis with a balance dot glowing 'truth green'. Chalk as a novice jumps at 0.19 s to the red side (42% wrong); an expert ghost waits until 0.27 s and follows the green dot.
Hick's law doors: a corridor with two doors takes one beat to choose; a feint paints a third fake door and the beat gets longer.
Youth timeline: a growing Tavi from 10 to 16 with reaction-time numbers ticking down (about 0.58 to 0.47 s for choices), and a caption that the half-turn is the one 'upgrade' you can install today.
Bonus teaser: freeze a step-over at -160, -80 and 0 ms. Reveal that with only upper body visible everyone guesses wrong, and with hips visible the truth appears late.
misconceptions: Folklore: 'The best players have faster reflexes.' Data: expert defenders start moving later (about 0.27 s vs 0.19 s for novices) and are fooled far less. They win by waiting and reading, not by twitching.

Folklore: 'Peripheral vision lets you see everything.' You detect movement at the edges but cannot read detail; acuity is one-sixteenth by 30 degrees, and nothing exists beyond about 107 degrees per eye. That is why you scan.
Folklore: 'You must see 360 degrees.' Nobody does. Side-on posture plus 0.4 s head turns covers what matters.

Folklore: 'More scanning is always better.' Scanning helps (small effect on pass completion, more turns and forward passes) but timing and quality matter, and scanning naturally drops under tight pressure.
Folklore: 'Nobody can react in under 0.1 s.' Instrumented starts show reaction under 100 ms in 20% of starts and neuromuscular components under 85 ms; the 0.100 s rule is a convention.

Folklore: 'Head up makes you dribble slower.' No study found that measures the trade-off directly; the evidence is that weaker young players look at the ball more and pros scan less while dribbling. Do not present a number for this.
Folklore: 'A big body feint is a good feint.' The centre of mass is the honest cue. Move it and skilled defenders read you; keep it quiet and exaggerate the parts that can lie.
Folklore: 'Back foot means the foot at the back.' It means the foot farther from the passer, whichever direction you face.

Folklore: 'Choice reaction times of youth players are about 0.4 s.' In large samples doing computer tasks, 10-16 year olds average roughly 0.47-0.58 s for a choice and 0.32-0.36 s for a simple reaction; lab minimums for adults are 0.21-0.22 s (simple) and about 0.48 s (choice). Name the task when quoting a number.

verdicts.claim: The human binocular visual field spans about 214 degrees horizontally; the temporal (outer) side of each eye reaches about 107 degrees.
verdicts.corrected_value: ~214 deg horizontal diameter (binocular); ~107 deg temporal per eye
verdicts.note: Strasburger, Rentschler and Juttner (2011), J Vis review. Verbatim: 'on the temporal side the visual field extends ... to around 107 deg' and 'up to around 214 deg horizontal diameter'. Adult perimetry data.

verdicts.claim: One eye sees about 60 degrees toward the nose and about 107 degrees away from the nose (Traquair perimetry).
verdicts.corrected_value: 60 deg nasal, 107 deg temporal, ~70 deg up, ~80 deg down
verdicts.note: Wikipedia quotes these values and attributes them to Traquair (1938). Secondary source, but it agrees with the Strasburger review.

verdicts.claim: Sharp detail is confined to the fovea: the foveola is about 1 degree across and the fovea about 5 degrees.
verdicts.corrected_value: foveola 1 deg; fovea 5.2 deg (Wandell 1995)
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Strasburger review.

verdicts.claim: Visual acuity falls to half the foveal value by about 2 degrees off centre and to about one-sixteenth at 30 degrees (E2 for letter acuity about 2.3 degrees).
verdicts.corrected_value: half at 2 deg; 1/16 at 30 deg (E2 ~2 deg); E2 for letter acuity 2.3 deg (Anstis 1974), grating 2.6-2.7 deg, Landolt C 1.0-1.1 deg
verdicts.note: Wikipedia text: 'At 2 deg, acuity is half the foveal value ... At 30 deg, it is one-sixteenth'. The 2.3 deg E2 is the Strasburger review's table value for letter acuity. Different acuity measures give E2 from 1.0 to 3.3 deg, so say 'about 2 degrees'.

verdicts.claim: Peripheral vision is relatively good at detecting motion and flicker (magnocellular pathway); the periphery is specialised for temporal sensitivity, and simple reaction time rises about 1.66 ms per degree of eccentricity.
verdicts.corrected_value: +1.66 ms/deg, measured out to +/-27 deg horizontally in 95 subjects aged 10-90
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the review, citing Poggel, Calmanti, Treutwein and Strasburger. Note the direction: the periphery detects motion well but reacts slightly slower per degree. The story does not claim it is faster, so no conflict.

verdicts.claim: In sport, players often anchor gaze in free space between information sources and use peripheral vision to monitor several players at once ('gaze anchor' / 'visual pivot').
verdicts.note: The paper at this DOI is Klostermann, Vater, Kredel and Hossner (2020), Front Sports Act Living 1:66, not a Vater first-author paper. Terminology: a 'visual pivot' is gaze placed between several sources; a 'gaze anchor' is gaze fixed at one functional spot (for example where the ball will be hit) while the periphery monitors. Quote: 'the visual pivot is optimally located in-between the relevant information sources'.

verdicts.claim: Vater, Williams and Hossner (2020) review the role of visual pivots and gaze anchors in sport (peripheral vision used for monitoring and motion detection). Full text was not retrievable in this session; DOI confirmed via Crossref.
verdicts.corrected_value: 'What do we see out of the corner of our eye? The role of visual pivots and gaze anchors in sport', Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol 13(1):81-103, online 2019, print 2020
verdicts.note: Crossref confirms title, authors, journal and pages. The full text is paywalled and not in Europe PMC, so only the citation is verified. Cite it for the concept, not for a number.

verdicts.claim: A saccade (eye jump) lasts about 20 to 200 ms depending on size, normal saccade latency is about 200 ms, and gaze shifts larger than about 20 degrees also recruit a head movement.
verdicts.corrected_value: 20-200 ms duration; ~200 ms latency to an unexpected stimulus; >20 deg with head
verdicts.note: Wikipedia matches. Secondary source, but these are textbook values.

verdicts.claim: In real 11v11 elite matches, one scan (head turn away from the ball) lasts on average 0.40 s (median 0.34 s); 90% of scans lasted 0.02-0.66 s; only 2.3% of scans contained a stable fixation, and those scans lasted about 0.97 s. Population: 4 Norwegian top-division central midfielders aged 17-23.
verdicts.corrected_value: mean 39.65 cs (0.3965 s); median 34 cs; 90.3% of scans between 2 and 66 cs; 20 scans (2.3%) with a fixation, M 97.10 cs
verdicts.note: Aksum, Brotangen, Bjorndal, Magnaguagno and Jordet, PLOS ONE 16(1), published 2021. 4 male central midfielders, 17-23 y (M 20.75), Eliteserien. Adult pros, tiny sample.

verdicts.claim: English Premier League players scanned 0.44 times per second before receiving; more scanning was associated with a higher probability of completing the pass (small effect, coefficient 0.13); players scanned least under tight pressure (0-1 m) and least before dribbling or shooting compared with passing. Population: 27 pros, 9,574 possessions.
verdicts.corrected_value: 0.44 +/- 0.30 scans/s; group coefficient 0.13 +/- 0.06 [0.02, 0.24]; by next action: pass 0.45, dribble 0.39, receive/touch 0.35, finish 0.27 scans/s
verdicts.note: Jordet et al. 2020. 27 pros aged 17-32 (M 25.66), 21 home matches. Dribbling is not the lowest category: finishing is lowest (0.27/s) and a plain touch/receive (0.35/s) is below dribbling (0.39/s). Pressure: lowest at 0-1 m, rising to about 4 m, d = 0.57 between 0-1 m and 10+ m. Say 'less before dribbling and least before shooting'.

verdicts.claim: Semi-elite players (16-30 y) turned their heads 1.44 times per second in the last second before receiving; players who explored more were more likely to turn with the ball, pass forward, and play to the side opposite to where the ball came from.
verdicts.corrected_value: 1.44 (SD 0.53) turns/s in the final 1 s; 0.95 (0.21) turns/s over 10 s
verdicts.note: McGuckian et al. 2018. 32 male semi-elite Australian NPL players, M 19.03 y. Effects are within-player odds ratios: turning linked to the final 1-2 s of exploration, forward passing to the 4-9 s window. Adults and older teens, not U12.

verdicts.claim: Competitive-elite youth players (mean 16.25 y) explored most when in possession and in the back third, and least during transitions and in the middle third.
verdicts.note: McGuckian, Cole, Chalkley, Jordet and Pepping 2020, J Sports Sci 38(6):658-668. 22 players, 1,623 min. Verified through the Europe PMC abstract because the publisher blocked the fetch.

verdicts.claim: A scanning training programme (4v4 game formats and passing exercises that reward recognising visual cues) raised scanning in U19 female players from 0.88 to 1.44 scans per game situation, with gains kept after 3 weeks; elite players improved more than grassroots.
verdicts.note: Hintermann et al. 2025. 36 female players, M 16.7 +/- 1.2 y, 5 weeks, 1-2 sessions/week with a 30 min scanning block. Caveat: the control group also rose (0.61 to 0.92), so the net training effect is smaller than the raw jump. Elite improved significantly (p = 0.001); grassroots did not reach significance.

verdicts.claim: Among 8-10 year old players doing a passing test with eye tracking, the lower-performing group looked more at the ball while handling it; gaze strategies develop alongside technical skill.
verdicts.note: Vansteenkiste, Lenoir, Krejtz and Krejtz 2022, J Eye Mov Res 15(1). Pilot study: 11 children, 5 high vs 6 low performers on the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test. Wording is 'tended to look more at the ball'. Very small sample. Present as a hint, not a rule.

verdicts.claim: No study was found that directly measures how much dribbling speed drops when a player looks up versus at the ball. 'Head up' is supported indirectly: better young players look at the ball less, pros scan less while dribbling than before passing, and elite U12-U16 players' response time to visual targets while passing improves about 30 ms per year. Treat 'head up costs speed' or 'head up is free' as unmeasured.
verdicts.note: Negative claim. None of the checked sources measures the trade-off. The three indirect supports are confirmed (Vansteenkiste 2022, Jordet 2020, Hicheur 2017). Keep it unmeasured and give no number.

verdicts.claim: Elite U12 players (11.6 y) needed about 1100 ms to react to a visual target and pass to it; U15/U16 players about 1027 ms; response time improved about 30 ms per year of age, passing speed 2.3 km/h per year.
verdicts.note: Hicheur et al. 2017 (COGNIFOOT). This 'response time' covers seeing the target, adjusting and completing the pass. It is a whole-action time, not a reaction time. Do not compare it with 0.2 s button-press values.

verdicts.claim: Adult simple visual reaction time (button press) is about 213-220 ms after correcting for hardware delay; it slows about 0.5 ms per year of adult age. Population: 1,469 adults 18-65.
verdicts.corrected_value: Exp 1: 231 ms raw, 213 ms corrected, slope 0.55 ms/y, youngest group 217.9 ms; Exp 2 (n 189, 18-82 y): 220 ms corrected, 0.45 ms/y
verdicts.note: Woods et al. 2015, Front Hum Neurosci.

verdicts.claim: Adult choice reaction time in a visual choice task was about 476 ms in the youngest adult group (mean 550 ms across 18-65), so choosing adds roughly 300 ms over a simple reaction.
verdicts.corrected_value: youngest group 476 ms (text) / 472 ms (Table 2); overall 550 ms; central processing time mean 319.1 ms; n 1,466
verdicts.note: Woods et al. 2015. The task is a two-button feature-conjunction task with adaptive pacing. The ~300 ms choice cost belongs to this task. Simpler two-choice tasks add less (Hick's law). Do not call 0.48 s a general 'lab minimum' for choice reactions.

verdicts.claim: In 38,778 people aged 10-18 doing a computer battery, simple reaction time (Detection task) fell from about 363 ms at age 10 to about 324 ms at 14-16 (log10 2.56 -> 2.51), and choice reaction time (Identification task) from about 575 ms at 10 to about 468 ms at 16 (log10 2.76 -> 2.67); speed reached adult level around 17-18.
verdicts.note: Cromer, Schembri, Harel and Maruff 2015, Cogstate Brief Battery. Conversions check out. Detection (psychomotor speed) plateaued at 13-14 y; the overall speed composite plateaued at 17-18 y. Computer key-press task, so values run above lab minimums.

verdicts.claim: Hick's law: decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices (Hick 1952, Hyman 1953).
verdicts.corrected_value: T = b log2(n + 1)
verdicts.note: Hick, Q J Exp Psychol 4(1):11-26 (1952); Hyman, J Exp Psychol 45(3):188-196 (1953).

verdicts.claim: World Athletics Technical Rules (Rule 16, The Start): a certified Start Information System flags a possible false start 'when the reaction time is less than 0.100 second' (Book C, C2.1, false-start section; Rules 16.7 and 16.8 cover false starts).
verdicts.corrected_value: 'System indicates a possible false start (i.e. when the reaction time is less than 0.100 second)'
verdicts.note: Verified in the C1.1 & C2.1 Competition Rules & Technical Rules PDF (last modified 1 July 2026). The sentence sits in the 'False Start' guidance paragraph, which points to Rules 16.7 and 16.8 of the Technical Rules. It is explanatory text next to the rule, not the numbered rule sentence itself.

verdicts.claim: The 0.1 s threshold is a convention, not a hard human limit: in instrumented sprint starts, 20% of starts in two conditions were under 100 ms, the neuromuscular component can be under 85 ms and EMG latencies under 60 ms.
verdicts.corrected_value: '20% of all starts in the first two conditions had a reaction time of less than 100 ms'; neuromuscular component <85 ms; EMG latencies <60 ms; 5 athletes averaged <100 ms in at least one condition
verdicts.note: Pain and Hibbs 2007, J Sports Sci 25(1):79-86. Small lab sample of trained sprinters. Verified through the Europe PMC abstract.

verdicts.claim: Wikipedia summary of the false-start rule and the physiological rationale (brain cannot process the gun in under 0.10 s), with citations to sprinters occasionally reacting in 0.08 s.
verdicts.note: Page states the 0.10 s rationale and cites a 2009 IAAF-commissioned study that top sprinters can sometimes react in 0.08 s. Secondary source. Use Pain and Hibbs for the number.

verdicts.claim: Adolescent male soccer players: a 505 test (5 m out, 180-degree turn, 5 m back) took 2.63 s at age 11.5 (pre-PHV), 2.55 s at 13.0 (circa-PHV) and 2.38 s at 15.4 (post-PHV), versus 10 m sprints of 2.06, 1.89 and 1.77 s; the change-of-direction deficit (turn cost) was 0.56, 0.66 and 0.61 s.
verdicts.note: Sert, Turgut Kaymakci, Gelen and Yildiz 2026, BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil (PMC13277277). Table values match exactly. Test is a full-speed run and turn without a ball.

verdicts.claim: Youth soccer U15-U18 (14.4-17.3 y): even a 90-degree turn in a 5 m + 5 m course cost 0.45-0.57 s more than a 10 m sprint (COD deficit), with total times 2.23-2.39 s versus 1.75-1.83 s straight.
verdicts.corrected_value: ages 14.42-17.33 y; 10 m 1.75-1.83 s; 90 deg COD total 2.23-2.39 s; deficit 0.45-0.51 s dominant, 0.52-0.57 s non-dominant
verdicts.note: Trecroci et al. 2020, PeerJ 8:e9486 (PMC7391970). 68 sub-elite players. Table values match.

verdicts.claim: Sharper change-of-direction angles need lower approach speed, longer braking distance, longer ground contact times and greater braking forces in the penultimate and final steps (angle-velocity trade-off); 180-degree turns are multi-step actions.
verdicts.corrected_value: GCT ~0.16-0.24 s at 45 deg vs 0.42-0.52 s at 180 deg; deceleration distance 7.1 m (90 deg) vs 4.3 m (45 deg)
verdicts.note: Dos'Santos, Thomas, Comfort and Jones 2018, Sports Med 48(10):2235-2253 (PMC6132493). Full text confirms each element, including the pivotal role of the penultimate foot contact in sharper turns.

verdicts.claim: Faster 180-degree turners (modified 505) have shorter final ground contact times, lower vertical impact forces and do more of their braking on the penultimate step.
verdicts.note: Dos'Santos, Thomas, Jones and Comfort 2017, JSCR 31(3):696-705. 40 adult male multidirectional athletes. Abstract: shorter FINAL GCT, lower vertical impact force, greater braking proportion in the penultimate contact 'may be advantageous'.

verdicts.claim: The COD deficit (505 time minus sprint time) isolates turning ability from straight speed (Nimphius et al. 2016).
verdicts.note: Nimphius, Callaghan, Spiteri and Lockie 2016, JSCR. 17 cricketers. COD deficit = 505 time minus 10 m time.

verdicts.claim: In a soccer-player biomechanics study, 88% of participants exceeded ACL injury-risk thresholds during 180-degree tasks versus 19% at 45 degrees, so sharp turns should be taught with bent knees and progressive loading.
verdicts.corrected_value: 19% (45 deg), 42% (90 deg), 73% (135 deg), 88% (180 deg); 26 male semi-professional players, mean age 23.4 +/- 2.8 y
verdicts.note: Li and Qian 2025, Sci Rep 15 (PMC12749382). Numbers hold, but the participants are adults, not youth. The paper recommends 'progressive eccentric strengthening, neuromuscular control training, and technique modification targeting reduced knee abduction moments'. 'Bent knees' is a paraphrase, not the paper's wording. Thresholds: dynamic valgus index >5.0 and knee abduction moment >2.0 N.m/kg for high risk.

verdicts.claim: A feint in a life-size video reactive-agility test made Australian footballers 34% slower (about 509 ms longer agility time); movement time rose 197 ms in lower-standard players but only 62 ms in higher-standard players.
verdicts.corrected_value: +34% (509 +/- 243 ms) agility time; movement time +62 +/- 86 ms (higher) vs +197 +/- 91 ms (lower)
verdicts.note: Henry, Dawson, Lay and Young 2012, J Sports Sci. 14 higher- and 14 lower-standard adult Australian footballers.

verdicts.claim: In a virtual-reality rugby side-step, novice defenders moved the wrong way 41.9% of the time versus 14.2% for experts; novices started moving earlier (about 193 ms) than experts (about 268 ms), who waited for honest information. Honest cues: centre-of-mass displacement and lower-trunk yaw. Deceptive cues: out-foot placement, head and upper-trunk yaw.
verdicts.corrected_value: 41.87% vs 14.16% wrong-way movements; initiation 192.71 ms (novices) vs 267.74 ms (experts)
verdicts.note: Brault, Bideau, Kulpa and Craig 2012, PLOS ONE. 12 experts vs 12 novices in the action experiment. Adults. Expert attunement to honest cues is inferred from behaviour; no eye tracking.

verdicts.claim: Skilled rugby attackers fool defenders by exaggerating head and upper-trunk movement while minimising centre-of-mass and lower-trunk movement ('balancing deceit and disguise').
verdicts.note: Brault, Bideau, Craig and Kulpa 2010, Hum Mov Sci 29(3):412-425. Abstract: COM displacement and lower trunk yaw minimised; foot displacement, head and upper trunk yaw exaggerated.

verdicts.claim: A basketball head fake slows the defender's response by about 56 ms in dynamic video (6 ms with static pictures); experts resist deception better but are not immune (review of deceptive actions in sport).
verdicts.corrected_value: 56 ms (video) vs 6 ms (static), from Alhaj Ahmad Alaboud et al. 2016
verdicts.note: Guldenpenning, Kunde and Weigelt 2017 review. The 56 ms is a response-time cost in a lab pass-direction task, not on court. Review states experts outperform novices but both are impaired by deceptive actions.

verdicts.claim: For soccer step-overs, viewers read normal moves correctly 88.6% of the time but deceptive moves only 32.2%; lower-skilled players were worse than chance until the foot touched the ball (0 ms), higher-skilled players only until 80 ms before contact.
verdicts.corrected_value: normal 88.6% (SD 6.5); deceptive 32.2% (SD 18.1); below chance: LS at -160, -80 and 0 ms; HS at -160 and -80 ms
verdicts.note: Wright and Jackson 2014, PLOS ONE. 27 higher-skilled (20.9 y) and 20 lower-skilled (22.6 y) adult males.

verdicts.claim: In step-over judgements, upper-body information matters early and lower-body (hips down) information dominates later; low-skilled players are biased toward believing a move is genuine.
verdicts.note: Jackson, Barton, Ashford and Abernethy 2018. Sensitivity at early occlusion higher with full/upper body; after foot-ball contact it rose more with full/lower body. 'Low-skilled players were more biased toward judging actions to be genuine.'

verdicts.claim: A single feint 'buys' roughly a quarter to half a second: defender simple reaction about 0.2-0.27 s (Woods; Brault initiation times) plus the extra 0.06-0.2 s of movement time and up to 0.5 s of total agility time a feint adds (Henry). This range is a synthesis across studies, not one measured number.
verdicts.note: No single study measures this. Each input is confirmed, but they come from different tasks and populations (adult button press, adult rugby VR, adult Australian football) and must not be added. Safe narration: 'In one test with adult footballers, a feint added about half a second.' Do not present 0.25-0.5 s as a measured range.
