mechanism_errors: Geometry vs turn angle: the story puts Sam on the left and the goal ahead, then compares a square receiver who 'spins 180 degrees'. In that setup a square receiver faces Sam and needs a 90 degree turn to face the goal, not 180. Either move Sam behind Tavi (back to goal) to justify 180, or use the 90 degree cost (0.45-0.57 s, ages 14-17).

Population mix in the turn costs: the 180 degree cost (0.56-0.66 s) is from 11.5-15.4 year olds (Sert 2026), but the 90 degree cost (0.45-0.57 s) is from 14.4-17.3 year old sub-elite players (Trecroci 2020). The story says 'even a 90 degree turn' right after '11 to 15 year old players', which implies one population.

The COD deficit is an analogy, not a measurement of the receiving turn. Both tests are full-speed runs without a ball, with the turn cost measured against a 10 m sprint. A player who receives square and turns with the ball starts near stationary. Present it as 'a run-and-turn test shows what a turn costs', not as the cost of turning after a receive.

'His alarm covers the passer and nothing else' overstates the loss. With a 214 degree field, a goal at 90 degrees to the side is still inside the far periphery (temporal edge ~107 degrees). What is lost is detail and the space behind him. Say 'the goal sits at the very edge, where he can only sense movement'.
'A defender covers about three metres in that time' is a derived estimate (0.5-0.6 s x 5-6 m/s), not a sourced figure. It is reasonable for a running teenager but label it as an estimate.

'With a choice between options, it takes about half a second' and the misconception text's 'about 0.48 s (choice)' come from one adult two-button feature task (Woods 2015: 472-550 ms). Simpler two-choice tasks are faster (Hick's law). Do not present 0.48 s as a lab minimum for choice reactions. Name the task.

The feint numbers are adult data: the half-second agility cost is from adult Australian footballers (Henry 2012), the 42% wrong-way rate is from adult rugby novices in virtual reality (Brault 2012), and the 88.6% vs 32.2% step-over reading is from adult male players (Wright and Jackson 2014). None is youth data. Name the population each time.

'Expert defenders wait and watch those' mixes a measured fact (experts initiated later, 268 vs 193 ms) with an inference (that they visually attend to hips and centre of mass). Brault 2012 had no eye tracking. Say 'experts wait and are better at reading the hips and body weight'.

The 'quarter to half a second a feint buys' range is a synthesis across three unrelated adult tasks and must not be narrated as a measured range. Quote the single measured value (about 0.5 s added agility time in one adult test) instead.

The ACL 88% vs 19% figures (Li and Qian 2025) come from 26 adult semi-professional men (23.4 y). The paper recommends eccentric strengthening, neuromuscular control training and technique changes that reduce knee abduction moments. 'Bent knees' is a paraphrase, not the paper's wording. Do not attach these percentages to U12 or U16 players.

The scanning-training result (0.88 to 1.44) should be read against the control group, which also rose from 0.61 to 0.92 without the programme. The net effect is smaller than the raw jump suggests, and the gain was significant only in the elite group.

The 1100 ms U12 'response time' (Hicheur 2017) covers seeing a target, adjusting and completing a pass. It is a whole-action time. Do not place it on the same scale as 0.2 s button-press reaction times.

Minor terminology: a 'gaze anchor' is gaze parked at one functional spot while the periphery monitors; a 'visual pivot' is gaze placed between several sources. The paper at DOI 10.3389/fspor.2019.00066 is Klostermann, Vater, Kredel and Hossner (2020), not a Vater first-author paper.
safe_numbers_for_narration: Adult vision science: the two eyes together cover about 214 degrees side to side. Each eye reaches about 107 degrees to the outside and 60 degrees toward the nose. Nothing exists beyond that.
Adult vision science: sharp vision is a spot about 1 degree (foveola) to 5 degrees (fovea) wide. Two degrees off centre, acuity is half. Thirty degrees off centre, it is one sixteenth.
Adult pros (4 Norwegian top-division central midfielders, 17-23 y): one scan away from the ball lasted 0.40 s on average and 0.34 s at the median. Only 2.3% of scans held a steady fixation.

Adult pros (27 Premier League players, 9,574 possessions): 0.44 scans per second in the 10 s before receiving. More scanning went with a slightly higher chance of a completed pass. Scanning was lowest with an opponent within 1 m, and lowest before a shot (0.27/s) compared with a pass (0.45/s).

Semi-elite adults and older teens (32 Australian players, 16-30 y): 1.44 head turns per second in the last second before receiving. Players who scanned more than their own average turned with the ball and passed forward more often.

Youth females (36 players, mean 16.7 y, U19): five weeks of scanning-focused 4v4 games raised scans from 0.88 to 1.44 per situation, and the gain held three weeks later. The control group also rose from 0.61 to 0.92.
Youth boys (94 players, 11.5-15.4 y): a 5 m out, 180 degree turn, 5 m back test took 2.38-2.63 s, against 1.77-2.06 s for a straight 10 m. The turn cost 0.56-0.66 s.
Youth boys (68 sub-elite players, 14.4-17.3 y): a 90 degree turn in a 5 m plus 5 m course cost 0.45-0.57 s more than a straight 10 m sprint.
Adults (1,469 people, 18-65 y): simple visual reaction time with a button press is about 0.21-0.22 s after hardware correction. In a two-button choice task the same lab measured about 0.47-0.55 s.

Youth (38,778 people, 10-18 y, computer tasks): simple reaction fell from about 0.36 s at age 10 to about 0.32 s by 14-16. Choice reaction fell from about 0.58 s at 10 to about 0.47 s at 16. Adult level arrived around 17-18.

Elite youth (Swiss academy players): U12 players (11.6 y) needed about 1.10 s to see a target and pass to it. U15/U16 players (14.7 y) needed about 1.03 s. The whole action got about 30 ms faster per year.

Adult Australian footballers (28 players): a feint on a life-size video screen made agility time 34% longer, about 0.51 s. Lower-standard players lost 197 ms of movement time to the feint; higher-standard players lost 62 ms.

Adult rugby players in virtual reality: novices moved the wrong way 42% of the time against a side-step; experts 14%. Experts started moving later (268 ms vs 193 ms). Honest cues were centre-of-mass shift and lower-trunk turn. Head, upper trunk and the outside foot could lie.
Adult soccer players (47 men): they read genuine moves correctly 88.6% of the time but step-overs only 32.2% of the time.

Athletics rule (World Athletics Book C): the start system flags a possible false start when reaction time is under 0.100 s. In a lab study of trained sprinters, 20% of starts in two conditions were under 100 ms, so the limit is a convention.
Adult semi-professional soccer men (26 players, 23 y): 88% exceeded ACL-risk thresholds on 180 degree turns, 73% at 135 degrees, 42% at 90 degrees and 19% at 45 degrees.

research.topic: Coaching frame: "time and space" in football. How coaches and coach education express it, the evidence that scanning, first touch and body shape separate levels in youth football, what youth curricula (FA, KNVB, FIFA Training Centre, US Youth Soccer, UEFA) say by age, what a well-run session looks like, how much time a player really has on the ball, and solo/pair drills for U12, U14 and U16.
research.one_line_hook: The best players are not faster than you. They finish thinking before the ball arrives, so they get to walk while everyone else sprints.
research.mechanism_story:
Picture Tavi standing still while the ball rolls toward him. Chalk, the chalk keeper, is sprinting in. Draw a ring around Tavi. The ring is not distance. It is time: how many seconds until Chalk reaches the ball. Far defender, big ring. Close and fast defender, tiny ring. Every good habit in football either makes that ring bigger or spends it wisely.

Step one is the look. Premier League players turn their head away from the ball about three times in the ten seconds before it arrives. Each look lasts less than half a second, and the eyes barely stop on anything. That is fine, because the outer part of your eyesight is built to spot movement, not detail. One quick turn and your brain already knows where the free teammate and the nearest threat are. Players who looked most often completed about 73 percent of their passes. Players who looked least completed about 54 percent. The look does not make you faster. It lets you decide before the ball comes, so you look calm when it does.

Step two is the touch. A ball meeting your foot is like two cars meeting. What matters is the speed difference between them. A stiff foot facing a fast ball is a big difference, so the ball springs off and rolls away. A foot that gives, moving back a little as the ball lands, shrinks that difference, and the ball dies at your feet. Once you can kill the bounce, you can aim it. One touch that rolls two or three metres away from the defender rolls him right out of your ring. Pro players keep the ball about one second per possession, two touches. The first touch decides what the second one can be.

Step three is the shape. Your eyes cover roughly a half circle, a bit more. Face the passer square-on and the goal is behind you, invisible. Stand side-on, and the ball and the goal both sit inside that half circle at the same time. Take the ball on the foot furthest from the passer, the back foot, and your first touch already faces forward. No extra turn, no extra second lost.

The bonus: a defender's brain needs about a fifth to a quarter of a second to read a move and start reacting. Expert defenders even wait longer on purpose, because early reactions get fooled. A shoulder drop sells a lie in less time than that. He steps, you go the other way, and you just stole time. That is why the best players look slow. They stopped racing the ball. They bought the time to walk.
plain_metaphors: The time bubble: a ring around the player that shows seconds, not metres. Distance divided by how fast the nearest defender can close. A big ring means you can walk. A tiny ring means one touch and gone.
Speed vs insight (Cruyff's idea): two runners, one starts a step earlier because he read the play. He looks faster. He is not. He just left first.
The look is a camera flash: a head turn shorter than half a second, and the eyes do not even need to stop. Peripheral vision is a motion detector, not a camera lens.
The first touch is two cars meeting: what matters is the speed difference. A parked car gets hit hard. A car rolling the same way gets a gentle bump. A giving foot is the rolling car.

The half circle of sight: hold your arms straight out to the sides. Roughly everything between your hands is visible. Face the passer and the goal is outside your hands. Turn side-on and both fit inside.
Two touches and one second: that is a pro possession. The first touch is the steering wheel. The second touch is the pass.
The defender's quarter second: a body feint is a lie told faster than a brain can check it.
Chasing the ball is a symptom: Cruyff said a player who has to chase the ball started running too late. The best players arrive, they do not chase.

jargon_map.plain_version: Turning your head away from the ball to look at teammates and defenders before the ball gets to you.
How many looks you take each second in the moments before you receive the ball.
The outside edge of what you can see without moving your eyes. Good at spotting movement, bad at detail.
When your eyes stop on one thing for a moment. Football scans are so quick they almost never contain one.
The full width you can see with both eyes. About 200 to 220 degrees, a bit more than a half circle.

jargon_map.term: First touch / ball reception / cushion control
jargon_map.plain_version: The first contact that stops or steers a ball coming to you.
How bouncy a collision is. It compares the speed the two things separate with the speed they came together.
Standing side-on when the ball comes, so you can see the passer and the way you want to play at the same time.
The foot furthest from the passer. Receiving on it means your first touch already points forward.
A keep-ball game where more attackers than defenders pass in a small square. Example: 4v1 or 5v2.
A practice rule: you may touch the ball at most twice before you pass it.
A match with fewer players and a smaller pitch, like 3v3 or 6v6.
The time from when you get the ball to when you give it away. About one second for a pro.
A fake move with your shoulders, hips or a foot that makes the defender guess wrong.
How long it takes to notice one signal and start moving. About a fifth of a second for adults.
How close the nearest defender is. Under one metre is tight. Four metres or more is loose.

claims.claim: Premier League players (27 players, one club, 21 matches, 9,574 possessions) scanned on average 3.0 times in the 10 seconds before receiving the ball, a mean of 0.44 scans per second. Population: adult pros.

In the same Premier League study, scanning dropped substantially under tight pressure (defender 0-1 m) compared with loose pressure (4 m or more), medium effect (d = 0.57). Players scanned more before long penetrative passes. Central midfielders and defenders scanned most, forwards least.

In Jordet, Bloomfield and Heijmerikx (2013), 118 Premier League midfielders and forwards in 1,279 situations: pass completion was 53.7% for low scan frequency (0-0.20 scans/s), 61.0% for medium (0.21-0.40), and 72.6% for high (0.41-1.80). Odds ratio 2.29 for the high group. Population: adult pros.

Same 2013 study: for midfielders making forward passes, completion rose from 38.2% (little scanning) to 73.2% (much scanning), odds ratio 4.42. Award-winning players scanned 0.33 scans/s vs 0.27 for others. Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard had the highest frequency at 0.62 scans/s.

Xavi quote, from Sid Lowe's Guardian interview (11 Feb 2011) as reproduced in Jordet et al. 2013: "When you arrive at Barca the first thing they teach you is: think. Think, think, think. Quickly. Lift your head up, move, see, think. Look before you get the ball." The Guardian page itself could not be fetched in this session, so wording is verified only through the Jordet paper's reproduction.

Eye-tracking of 4 elite Norwegian top-division central midfielders (869 scans): mean scan duration 0.40 s, median 0.34 s, 90.3% of scans lasted 0.66 s or less, and only 2.3% of scans contained a fixation (120 ms threshold). Authors conclude players gather scan information with peripheral vision rather than by fixating. Population: adult pros.
claims.value: mean 0.40 s; median 0.34 s; 2.3% with fixation

claims.claim: Eye-tracking of 5 elite Norwegian central midfielders in 11v11 (2,832 fixations): mean fixation duration 242 ms; players fixated longer when several objects (ball, opponent, teammate) were in view together.

Semi-elite players (32 men, 16-30 y, 783 possessions) wearing a head sensor in 11v11: head-turn frequency rose from about 0.95 turns/s ten seconds before possession to 1.44 turns/s one second before. Higher-than-usual head-turn excursion before receiving predicted turning with the ball; higher frequency predicted forward passes. Pass success itself was not significantly linked. Note: sensor 'head turns' count more events than video 'scans'.

Competitive-elite youth players (22 players, mean age 16.25 y, 1,623 minutes of 11v11): players explored most in the back third of the pitch, least in the middle third, more when in possession, and less during transitions. Population: elite youth, about U17.

UEFA U17 and U19 Championship semi-finals and finals (53 outfield players, 1,686 attacking situations): U19 players scanned more than U17 players; central midfielders and central defenders scanned most; there was a positive relationship between scan frequency and pass success; opponent pressure and pitch position shaped scanning. Population: elite youth.

UEFA U17, U19 and U21 Championships (239 players, 17 matches): positive relation between scanning frequency and successful passes; opponent pressure had a large effect on pass result and on the player's body orientation. Population: elite youth.

UEFA U17 and U21 Championship 2019 (162 players, 9 matches): when a player's last scan before receiving goes to the side of the dominant foot, the probability rises that the dominant foot makes the first ball contact. Body shape and the last look are linked.

Euro 2016 midfielders (35 players): scan rate correlated positively with passing percentage but explained only about 3-4% of the variance (R-squared 3.0-4.0%). Scanning helps, but it is a small part of pass success at pro level. Population: adult pros.

Elite youth female players (25 players, mean 17.6 y) in 4v4 games: verbal cues to scan for teammates, opponents and space before receiving increased scans before reception by 27% (rate ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.12-1.44). Players who made at least one scan were 3.4 times more likely to have a successful next action (OR 3.40, 95% CI 2.59-4.62). Population: elite youth, female.

"Heads Up Girls!" five-week scanning programme (36 U19 female players, mean 16.7 y, elite and grassroots Swiss teams, 4v4-based): scanning rose from 0.88 to 1.44 scans per game situation in the trained group (p = 0.002) and was kept at a 3-week retention test. Elite players improved (1.06 to 1.72); grassroots players did not change significantly. Outcomes were positive 70.6% of the time when the player scanned before first contact vs 62.5% when not. Population: youth, female.

Elite youth female players (39 players, mean 17.45 y, Swiss U19 league, 4 matches, 819 events): 0.27 scans/s before reception and 0.61 scans/s during possession; mean possession 1.62 s; each extra 0.1 scans/s during possession raised the odds of a successful pass by about 9% (OR 1.09). Tight opponent pressure cut the odds of a successful dribble by 92%. Scan timing within the 10 s window showed no association. Population: elite youth, female.

Jordet's 2005 imagery training study with elite players showed exploratory behaviour is trainable in a few weeks, with immediate increases in exploration frequency and, for some players, immediate performance gains (as summarised in Jordet et al. 2013).

Pocock et al. (2019) used an imagery intervention to train visual exploratory activity in elite academy football players (Journal of Applied Sport Psychology). Not fetched in this session; cite only as existing.

French Ligue 1 (28 players, 30 matches): a player was in possession of the ball for 53.4 +/- 8.1 s per match, with 1.1 +/- 0.1 s and 2.0 +/- 0.2 touches per possession, covering 4.2 m per possession and 191 m with the ball per match. Speed at ball reception 10.3 km/h. Population: adult pros.
claims.value: 53.4 s per match; 1.1 s and 2.0 touches per possession

claims.claim: German Bundesliga 2013/14 (60 matches): a player had 'individual ball control' (enough control to choose between options) for 1 min 21 s on average per match; central forwards least (0:49), central defenders and goalkeepers most (1:38); about 836 individual ball-control intervals per match. Population: adult pros.

Young players (34 boys, 13 +/- 0.9 y): 3v3 on 15x25 m produced significantly more short passes, kicks, tackles, dribbles and goals per game than 6v6 on 30x40 m; heart rate 87.6% vs 82.8% of maximum. Population: youth, about U14.

Pre-pubescent players (about 11 y): 7v7 on 60x40 m produced significantly more passes and fewer tackles than 11v11 on 100x65 m; heart rate above 170 bpm 84% of the time in both. Population: youth, about U12.

Scottish Premier League players (15 pros): 3v3 gave significantly more ball contacts per player than 9v9 (large effect), with more dribbles, shots and tackles and fewer passes, receives and headers. Population: adult pros.

Elite players (18 +/- 1 y): changing 5v5 pitch size from 30x20 to 50x40 m did not change heart rate or most technical actions, but tackles and shots fell as the pitch grew (tackles 45 vs 15; shots 85, 60, 44). Pitch size is a dial for pressure. Population: elite youth/young adults.

U15 players (28 boys, about 12.9 y): experienced players (about 4 years of practice) built longer attacking sequences with more ball circulation; inexperienced players produced faster sequences dominated by individual actions; 3v3 vs 6v6 changed the pattern in both groups. Population: youth, U13-U15.

Junior players in 4v4 with goalkeepers (12 males, 30 games): a 2- or 3-touch limit increased pass frequency, while free play produced more receptions; time between first and second touch was shortest in the attacking zone. Population: junior amateurs.

Review of touch restrictions in small-sided games (2025): 1-touch and 2-touch rules raise the number of passes and physical intensity (more sprinting and high-intensity running), but effects on pass success are mixed, and evidence on tactical effects across age groups is scarce.

Ghent Youth Soccer Project (U13 n=117, U14 n=136, U15 n=138, U16 n=99; elite, sub-elite, non-elite): at U13 and U14, running speed and technical skills were the most important discriminators between levels; at U15 and U16, cardiorespiratory endurance also mattered. Population: youth, Belgian.

Dutch talented players aged 14-18 (131 players): those who later became professionals were 0.3 s faster on 30 m peak dribbling and about 1 s faster on 3x30 m repeated dribbling than those who stayed amateur. Population: elite youth.

Longitudinal study of 267 talented players aged 12-19: from 14 to 16 sprinting improved rapidly while dribbling did not; after 16 dribbling improved considerably and sprinting hardly changed. Skill and speed develop on different clocks. Population: elite youth.

Elite young players (U14 n=14, U16 n=22, U18 n=25): acceleration, maximum running speed and repeated-sprint ability improved with age group, but the differences disappeared once biological maturity (age at peak height velocity) was accounted for. Population: elite youth.

Elite U12-U16 match play (112 players, 14 matches): flying 10 m sprint times were U12 1.58 s, U13 1.52 s, U14 1.51 s, U15 1.35 s, U16 1.31 s, that is roughly 6.3 m/s at U12 rising to about 7.6 m/s at U16. Useful for the time-bubble: a defender 5 m away at full speed closes in under a second. Population: elite youth.

Roca, Williams and Ford (2012), 64 players (elite high-performers, elite low-performers, recreational): hours per year of soccer-specific play in childhood was the strongest predictor of anticipation and decision-making skill.

Williams and Davids (1998), 12 experienced vs 12 less experienced players: experienced players spent less time looking at the ball or passer and more time on other areas, and they relied on peripheral information about the positions and movements of other players.

Pilot eye-tracking study of 11 children aged 8-10 on the Loughborough Soccer Passing Test: the low-performance group tended to look more at the ball while handling it; gaze strategies develop alongside technical skill. Population: youth, U11.

Rugby side-step deception (virtual reality, 14 experts vs 14 novices, then 12 vs 12): experts waited longer before moving (268 ms vs 193 ms after movement onset) and were fooled far less often (14% vs 42% wrong-direction moves). Honest cue: centre-of-mass displacement. Deceptive cues: upper-trunk yaw, head yaw, outside-foot placement. Population: adult rugby players; transfer to football is by analogy.
claims.value: experts 268 ms vs novices 193 ms; 14% vs 42% fooled

claims.claim: Simple visual reaction time in adults (1,469 subjects aged 18-65) averages about 231 ms (213 ms after hardware correction), rising about 0.5 ms per year of age. Choice decisions take longer. Population: general adults, not athletes.

Simple reaction time in 8-9-year-old children averaged about 427 ms (SD 52) in one environmental-health cohort, roughly double the adult value, so young players react more slowly than adults. Cohort was not athletes; use as a rough order of magnitude only.

The normal monocular visual field extends about 60 degrees toward the nose and 107 degrees outward, about 70 degrees up and 80 degrees down; the fovea covers only the central 5.2 degrees. Combined binocular field is 200-220 degrees horizontally, a bit more than a half circle. Peripheral vision is relatively good at detecting motion and weak at detail, colour and shape.
Monocular field limits (60 nasal, 107 temporal, 70 up, 80 down) and fovea size (5.2 degrees; foveola 1-1.2 degrees) as summarised on Wikipedia's Visual field page.

In basketball defence 'it is impossible to keep track of all players without peripheral vision'; skilled athletes compensate for eccentricity effects through positioning and perceptual strategies. Supports the idea that body shape and where you stand decide what your periphery can catch.

Coefficient of restitution: the relative speed of separation after a collision divided by the relative speed of approach before it. It is a property of the two colliding surfaces, so a foot that moves back with the ball lowers the approach speed and the rebound speed, and the ball ends up moving slowly relative to the ground. No value for a football-foot impact is listed on the page.

Instep kick impact (adult players): foot-ball contact lasts about 9.0 +/- 0.4 ms, the ball deforms up to 6.2 cm, peak ball reaction force about 2,926 N. Foot-ball contact is a very short impact, which is why a stiff foot cannot 'catch' a ball; only a moving-back foot can reduce the rebound.

Law 2 (IFAB): the ball is 68-70 cm in circumference, 410-450 g at the start of the match, inflated to 0.6-1.1 atmosphere at sea level; official competition balls must carry a FIFA Quality Programme mark.

Cruyff (sourced to David Winner, Brilliant Orange): "Every trainer talks about movement, about running a lot. I say don't run so much. Football is a game you play with your brain. You have to be in the right place at the right moment, not too early, not too late."

Cruyff (sourced to Dennis Bergkamp, Stillness and Speed, 2013): "Because you play football with your head, and your legs are there to help you... Why does a player have to chase the ball? Because he started running too late. You have to pay attention, use your brain and find the right position. If you get to the ball late, it means you chose the wrong position. Bergkamp was never late."

Cruyff on speed vs insight (Dutch original in the Wikipedia collection of 'Cruijffiaans'): "Wat is snelheid? Vaak verwisselt de sportpers snelheid met inzicht. Kijk, als ik iets eerder begin te lopen dan een ander, dan lijk ik sneller." Translation: "What is speed? The sports press often confuses speed with insight. Look, if I start running a bit earlier than someone else, I seem faster." Also: "Als je ergens niet bent, ben je of te vroeg of te laat" (If you are not somewhere, you are either too early or too late) and "Voetballen is simpel. Het moeilijkste wat er is, is simpel voetballen." The page does not give an original date or interview, so treat exact wording as a widely repeated version, not a verified primary quote.

Cruyff on the rondo, as quoted in Stan Baker's book Our Competition is the World and reproduced by These Football Times and Soccer America: "Everything that goes on in a match, except shooting, you can do in a rondo. The competitive aspect, fighting to make space, what to do when in possession and what to do when you haven't got the ball, how to play 'one touch' football, how to counteract the tight marking and how to win the ball back." Secondary source; original date not verified.

Typical rondo formats and rules (coaching sources): 3v1, 4v1, 5v2, 5v5+2; often a 10x10 yard grid; the outnumbered defenders try to win or 'split' the circle; touch limit often 1-2 touches; when a defender wins the ball or splits the circle, he swaps with the player who lost it.

The FA (England Football Learning) receiving-under-pressure session for 7-11s coaches 'body shape before receiving', approaching 'at an angle' to 'receive and turn more easily', and positioning 'on the half-turn'; it uses a 3v2 into 3v3 format with a middle receiving zone, and scales pressure by pitch size and defender delay.

The FA's 7-11s 'moving with the ball and turning to attack' programme says: 'Before receiving, encourage your players to adopt an open body shape to allow them to turn and play forward if they have space'; 'Remind players to scan before, during, and after receiving the ball, so they know where and when to move and turn'; 'When near a defender, get players to think about taking smaller touches and keeping the ball close to them.'

The FA's 7-11s receiving-techniques session: players 'receive on the back foot outside the cone then pass'; 'Encourage your players to try to scan before receiving the ball'; 'Make sure they're looking at their teammates and opposition players'; one practice limits the receiver to two touches in a central box.

The FA lists receiving as one of ten core skills: it 'starts with learning where to stand to receive the ball and progresses to techniques like receiving on the half-turn or with their back to the opposition'; turning 'can even be as simple as changing body position to receive a pass or face an opponent'.

FIFA Training Centre, Christchurch United FC U-12 session 'Scan to play forward': players must 'frequently scan before and after each pass to recognise the best space to receive the ball in'; 'scanning frequently and using effective body orientation and signals helps promote forward play with speed'; built on a four-quadrant rondo, a passing-turning-receiving activation, and 3v3+2 games.

FIFA Training Centre grassroots essentials for ages 8-12 recommend numeric progression games (2v1, then 3v3, then 6v6 with zones) and state that 'possession-based games give players lots of time on the ball, building their confidence'.

FIFA Training Centre for ages 12-15: a three-phase progressive methodology (technical foundation with 'lots of repetition', tactical introduction with 'leading questions', game application with 'minimal coaching intervention'); it stresses 'a good first touch' and 'quick, effective decisions under pressure', and uses a 5v5 split into 4v1 halves.

KNVB formats: Onder 8-10 play 6v6 on about a quarter pitch (42.5 x 30 m) with no published standings and a 'spelbegeleider' (play guide) instead of a referee; Onder 11-12 play 8v8 on about half a pitch (42.5 x 64 m); Onder 13-19 play 11v11 with 'plezier en ontwikkeling' (enjoyment and development) first.
KNVB Onder 8-10: '6 tegen 6 wedstrijden op een bijna kwart veld (42,5m x 30m)'; results are deliberately not published because ranking pressure 'gaat ten koste van het spelplezier'.

US Youth Soccer Game Format Project moves U5-U6 to 2v2 or 3v3 because 'the 2v2 and 3v3 game formats allow players to have more touches on the ball than 4v4 or 5v5' and create 'more 1v1 opportunities'; coaches get the USYS National Curriculum through MOJO. The older 'Skills School' manual and US Soccer's Player Development Initiatives page could not be fetched in this session.

US Soccer's Player Development Initiatives (2015-2017) set small-sided standards of 4v4 for U6-U8, 7v7 for U9-U10, 9v9 for U11-U12 and 11v11 from U13, with a build-out line at 7v7. The official page returned 404 in this session, so this is from memory of the programme and is unverified here.

UEFA defines grassroots football as 'the foundation of the game' that 'prioritises the love of the football and joy of participation', 'non-professional and non-elite', and inclusive of everyone. UEFA's pages fetched here give no age-specific technical curriculum for receiving or awareness.

Jordet et al. (2013) practical advice: scouts 'should look at what players do when the ball is not around'; players should be encouraged 'particularly in the period prior to receiving the ball, to engage in extensive visual exploratory behavior using body, head and eyes, and maintain exploring until the ball is received'; close-up films of each player are an effective feedback tool.

Aksum et al. (2021) practical applications: coaches should 'consider creating exercises in which scans need to be performed quickly, in a dynamic affordance-rich environment', 'limit their use of non-contextual information that players need to fixate on during their scans' (for example coloured cones or numbers held up), and 'limit the delivery of unopposed exercises'.

technique_cues: Look before the ball leaves your teammate's foot, then one more quick look while it travels. Pros take about three looks in ten seconds.
Turn your head, not your whole body. A look should be shorter than half a second. You do not need to focus on anything. Let the edges of your eyes catch the movement.
Last look to the side you want to play. Your first touch will follow your eyes.
Arrive side-on. Ball on one side of your half circle, goal on the other.
Take it on the back foot, the foot furthest from the passer, so your first touch already points forward.
Give with the foot. Let the ankle and knee move back a little as the ball lands. Kill the speed difference, kill the bounce.
Touch away from pressure, never straight ahead by habit. Two or three metres to the side that has no defender buys you a second.
Near a defender, smaller touch. In space, bigger touch. Pitch size and pressure decide the size of the touch.
Check the defender's belly button, not his head or shoulders. The centre of the body tells the truth, the shoulders lie.
Sell the lie with your shoulders and a big fake step, then go the other way in one motion. A quarter second is all you need.
Play the pass you decided on before the ball came. If the picture changed, your one extra look while the ball travels tells you.
Slow down when you have time and speed up when you do not. Do not spend your time bubble on a sprint you never needed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Watching the ball all the way in with the head down.
common_mistakes.consequence: The picture is old by the time the ball arrives. You need an extra touch and an extra second to look up, and the defender uses that second.
common_mistakes.fix: Look when the ball is still far from you, then again as it travels. Trust your feet to find a ball you already saw.

common_mistakes.mistake: Receiving square-on, facing the passer.
common_mistakes.consequence: The goal is behind you, outside your half circle. Every forward option costs a full turn.
common_mistakes.fix: Arrive at an angle, side-on, hips open to the pitch. Receive on the back foot.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stiff, locked ankle when the ball arrives fast.
common_mistakes.consequence: Big speed difference between foot and ball, so the ball bounces a metre or more away and the defender pounces.
common_mistakes.fix: Soft ankle, let the foot travel back a little with the ball. Practise against a wall until the ball stops within a step.

common_mistakes.mistake: First touch straight in front of you, out of habit.
common_mistakes.consequence: Often straight into the defender's path. The touch adds no time.
common_mistakes.fix: Decide the touch direction from your last look. Touch away from pressure, two or three metres, into the space you saw.

common_mistakes.mistake: Scanning in an exaggerated, slow, full-body swivel.
common_mistakes.consequence: You are blind to the ball for too long and often mis-time the touch. Real scans are brief head turns.
common_mistakes.fix: Quick head flicks under half a second. Keep the ball in the edge of your vision. Frequency and timing matter more than how far you turn.

common_mistakes.mistake: Only scanning when unmarked.
common_mistakes.consequence: Pressure is exactly when the picture matters most, but studies show scanning drops under tight pressure.
common_mistakes.fix: Make pressure the trigger to look. In rondos, add a defender and keep the scan rule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a feint from the head, shoulders or fake foot.
common_mistakes.consequence: Those cues are the lie. Novices moved the wrong way about 42 percent of the time in a deception study.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the hips and belly button, and be patient. Experts waited about 75 ms longer and were fooled a third as often.

common_mistakes.mistake: Coaching scanning with numbers or coloured cones held up behind the player.
common_mistakes.consequence: Trains the player to fixate on non-football information. Real scans contain almost no fixations. Researchers advise limiting this.
common_mistakes.fix: Use real teammates and defenders as the information. Ask 'where was the free player' after the action instead.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing speed is the whole answer.
common_mistakes.consequence: Sprint speed jumps with puberty and not because of training. Skill and decision-making keep improving after 16 and separate future pros.
common_mistakes.fix: Train the look, the touch and the shape every session. Let growth take care of the legs.

drills: LOOK 1, Wall scan (solo). Stand 5-8 m from a wall in an open area away from windows and roads. Pass firmly, and while the ball returns turn your head to check a marker you placed behind you (a cone, a bag, a tree), then receive and pass again. Rule: one look per return. Safety: check the wall is solid and the ground is dry, dynamic warm-up first, size 4 ball for U12. U12: one look, 3 sets of 10 passes, ball can stop. U14: two looks (both shoulders), receive on the back foot, two-touch max. U16: two looks and call out what you saw before your touch, one-touch return when possible, 20 s work, 20 s rest, 6 rounds.

LOOK 2, Shoulder-check pass (pair). Partner 8-10 m away passes; you must look over both shoulders while the ball travels. Partner silently raises one hand as you look; your first touch must go to the side of the raised hand, then you pass back. Uses a real person as the information, not a cone. Safety: flat grass, agree pass strength, no driven balls at U12. U12: rolling passes, hand raised early. U14: firmer passes, hand raised late so the last look decides. U16: partner becomes a live defender who steps to one side as the ball travels; touch away from him, 3 sets of 10 each.

LOOK 3, Scan count from video (solo homework). Have a parent or friend film you for 10 minutes of a match or small-sided game, ideally zoomed on you like the Sky PlayerCam that the 2013 study used. At home, count your head turns in the 10 seconds before each ball you receive. Pro average is 3 looks in 10 seconds. Safety: none on the pitch; just keep phone use off the field. U12: target at least 1 look before every reception. U14: target 2 looks with the last one as the ball travels. U16: target 3 looks and note whether your first touch matched the space you saw.

TOUCH 1, Kill the bounce (solo). Drop the ball from waist height and cushion it with the inside of the foot so it does not bounce away. Then throw it up, let it bounce once, and cushion the rolling ball. Then play hard passes against a wall and cushion the return so the ball stops within one step. Safety: soft footwear or boots, not slippers; not on wet concrete; stay off roads. U12: ball must stop inside a 1 m circle, 3 sets of 10. U14: cushion then immediately move the ball 2 m to the side with the same foot. U16: cushion and steer in one touch to a target gate 3 m away at an angle, alternate feet, count successes out of 20.

TOUCH 2, Two-gate first touch (pair). Set two 1 m cone gates 3 m to your left and right. Partner passes from 10 m and, as the ball travels, points to one gate: that is the 'defender side'. Your first touch goes through the other gate, second touch is a pass back. Safety: stable cones or markers, not bottles; keep the area 3 m clear behind gates. U12: rolling pass, point early, two touches. U14: firmer pass, point late; alternate inside and outside of the foot. U16: partner shouts 'time' or 'man' instead of pointing; 'man' means touch away and pass first-time back; 'time' means touch forward and carry through the far gate, 4 sets of 8.

TOUCH 3, Bounce-ball and volley cushion (pair, U14 and up for hard balls). Partner throws or half-volleys a ball that arrives above ground; you take it out of the air with thigh or inside of foot so it drops dead, then pass. Safety: soft throws at first, no headers required, watch for other players behind the receiver, warm the hip flexors. U12: underarm throws to the thigh and foot only, ball can bounce once before control. U14: chest-height throws, control in one touch, ball must stay within a step. U16: partner drives a low kick from 15 m, cushion and play forward through a gate in two touches.

SHAPE 1, Back-foot square (solo with wall, or pair). Mark a 6 m square. Approach a cone at an angle so your body is side-on to the wall or partner, receive on the back foot so the ball ends in front of the far cone, then pass to a third cone. Safety: cones flat to the ground, no metal markers. U12: walking pace, freeze after the touch and check: can you see the passer and the third cone at once? U14: jogging, two touches max, alternate sides so both feet learn the half-turn. U16: partner passes from behind the shoulder line so you must find the half-turn quickly; add a timer, 45 s work, 30 s rest, 5 rounds.

SHAPE 2, Half-turn gate (pair). Partner stands 10 m behind and to the side; a target cone stands 10 m ahead. Rule: you may receive only when your body is side-on so that both the partner and the cone are inside your field of view. First touch forward, second touch hits the cone. Swap roles every 10. Safety: keep the target cone away from paths or other groups. U12: partner passes softly, you may stop the ball. U14: firmer pass and a passive 'shadow' defender standing behind you; touch away from him. U16: the shadow defender is live and can press when the ball is halfway to you; if he gets tight, play back first-time; if not, turn and go.

BONUS, Feint and steal a quarter second (pair). Partner passes and then jogs in to defend. Drop a shoulder and plant a fake step one way, take the ball the other way past him, and stop. Then swap and, as the defender, practise waiting and watching the attacker's hips rather than the shoulders. Safety: no tackles, no slide challenges, defender stays on his feet, shin pads for U12 and U14. U12: defender walks in; attacker chooses the direction in advance. U14: defender jogs and may block with body only; attacker decides late. U16: defender can win the ball with a fair toe poke; count how often the defender bites, then swap after 6.

SESSION FRAME for a coach or a group of friends (rondo 4v1 to 5v2). Square about 10x10 m (smaller for U16, bigger for U12). Attackers keep the ball, defenders win it; the defender who wins swaps with the player who lost it. Constraints from the research: scan before you receive (one look), two-touch max, then one-touch for U16, and add a second defender when the scan rule holds under pressure. Safety: no slide tackles, defenders stay on their feet, rotate defenders every 60-90 s to avoid fatigue collisions. U12: 4v1, free touches then two-touch. U14: 4v1 into 5v2, two-touch, receive on the half-turn. U16: 5v2, one-touch when possible, split-the-circle counts double for defenders.
animation_ideas: The time bubble: a glowing ring around Tavi with a countdown in seconds (distance to Chalk divided by Chalk's closing speed). As Chalk sprints in, the ring shrinks. A scan, a good touch or a half-turn each makes the ring swell back.

Split screen like the Sky PlayerCam: left side shows the whole pitch, right side a close-up of Tavi's head flicking left and right. A counter ticks: 1, 2, 3 looks in 10 seconds. Fade in a bar chart: 54%, 61%, 73% pass completion as the looks increase.

Speed vs insight: two runners on a track. One starts one frame earlier because he saw the pass coming. Freeze frame at the ball: same running speed, one metre difference. Cruyff line overlaid: 'If I start running earlier, I seem faster.'

Camera-flash scans: each head turn flashes for 0.4 seconds and paints a faint ghost image of every player's position in Tavi's mind. No zoom, no focus ring; the whole frame lights up, showing peripheral vision at work.
Two-cars collision: a rolling ball meets a locked steel foot and springs off; then meets a foot that rolls back with it and dies. A speedometer shows the speed difference dropping to nearly zero.
Time bought in metres: one first touch rolls 3 metres away from Chalk. A ruler unfolds and converts to seconds on the time bubble.
Half-circle of sight: a translucent 200-220 degree wedge drawn from Tavi's eyes. Square-on: the goal falls outside the wedge and goes dark. Side-on: passer and goal both light up inside the wedge.

Back-foot arrow: the ball arrives, Tavi takes it on the far foot and an arrow appears from the touch straight toward the goal. Replay with the near foot: the arrow curls back and a stopwatch adds a second.
Chalk's quarter second: freeze Chalk with a brain icon and a 250 ms progress bar while Tavi's shoulder drop plays at full speed. Chalk's feet move only when the bar fills, one step too late.

The 53-second hourglass: a whole 90-minute match compresses into an hourglass with only 53 seconds of sand labelled 'time you actually have the ball'. Each grain is one possession of about one second and two touches.
misconceptions: 'Players have the ball for minutes every game.' Pros have it about 53 seconds per match in Ligue 1 and about 1 minute 21 seconds of real control in the Bundesliga. Each possession is about one second and two touches.

'The best players are the fastest.' Sprint speed in youth is mostly maturation: age-group differences vanish when biological maturity is controlled. Dribbling skill keeps improving after 16 and separates future pros; Cruyff called speed 'often confused with insight'.
'Keep your eye on the ball.' Experienced players spend less time looking at the ball and passer and more on other players; low-performing 8-10-year-olds looked more at the ball while handling it.
'You see 180 degrees.' Normal binocular field is 200-220 degrees, a bit more than a half circle; the sharp centre is only about 5 degrees.

'Scanning means looking around a lot.' Scan frequency explains only about 3-4 percent of pass-success variance in Euro 2016 midfielders. Timing, pressure and body orientation matter alongside frequency, and one look before the ball already triples the odds of a good next action in youth players.
'Scans are long looks.' Elite scans last about 0.4 seconds and 98 percent contain no fixation at all; the periphery does the work.
'Watch the attacker's head and shoulders to read a feint.' Those are the deceptive cues. Centre of mass is honest, and experts wait longer before committing.

'Reaction time is a quarter second for everyone.' Adults: about 0.21-0.23 s for a simple reaction; choice decisions take longer; 8-9-year-olds are around 0.43 s. Kids' defenders are slower to react, so feints work even better at U12.

'4v4 gives 135% more passes than 8v8' (Manchester United pilot, often quoted). Folklore-level: I could not find the primary source this session. Peer-reviewed data do show more short passes, dribbles and contacts per player in 3v3 vs 6v6 (13-year-olds) and 3v3 vs 9v9 (pros), without those exact percentages.

'Two-touch rules always improve passing.' Reviews show more passes and higher intensity, but pass success results are mixed and free play gives more receptions; use the constraint for a purpose, not by default.

verdicts.claim: Premier League players (27 players, one club, 21 matches, 9,574 possessions) scanned 3.0 times in the 10 s before receiving, 0.44 scans/s.
verdicts.note: Paper text: 'on average 3.0 scans (±2.1) in the last 10 s before receiving the ball, giving a mean scan frequency of 0.44 scans/s (±0.30)'. 27 male pros aged 17-32, one EPL club, 21 home games (13 PL, 6 Europa League, 2 League Cup).

verdicts.claim: Same study: scanning dropped under tight pressure (0-1 m) vs loose pressure (4 m or more), d = 0.57; more scans before long penetrative passes; central midfielders and defenders scanned most, forwards least.
verdicts.corrected_value: d = 0.57 is for 0-1 m compared with 10+ m, not 4 m or more. Scan frequency about 0.38/s at 0-1 m vs about 0.46/s at 10+ m.
verdicts.note: Pressure bands were 0-1, 2, 3, 4, 5-6, 7-9 and 10+ m. Effect sizes ran from trivial (d = 0.04) to medium (d = 0.57, 0-1 m vs 10+ m). Central midfielders highest, central defenders second, forwards lowest (d = 0.55 CM vs forwards). Long penetrative passes confirmed. The paper also says the scan effect on pass completion is small next to technical ability and pass difficulty.

verdicts.claim: Jordet, Bloomfield and Heijmerikx (2013): 118 players, 1,279 situations; pass completion 53.7% (0-0.20 scans/s), 61.0% (0.21-0.40), 72.6% (0.41-1.80); OR 2.29.
verdicts.note: Read from the PDF text. Figure 1: 53.7% (ref), 61.0% (OR 1.35, p = .028), 72.6% (OR 2.29, p < .001). Midfielders and forwards only. Correlational, not causal.

verdicts.claim: Same study: midfielders' forward-pass completion 38.2% to 73.2%, OR 4.42; award winners 0.33 vs 0.27 scans/s; Lampard and Gerrard 0.62 scans/s.
verdicts.note: Exact text: 'Midfield players that explore little only complete 38.2% of their forward passes, compared to 73.2% when they explore much (OR = 4.42, p < .001)'. Award winners M = .33 (SD .25) vs .27 (SD .22). Lampard and Gerrard both M = .62.

verdicts.claim: Xavi quote from Sid Lowe's Guardian interview (11 Feb 2011), reproduced in Jordet et al. 2013.
verdicts.note: Fetched through a text proxy this session. Guardian text: 'The difference between them and us is we have more players who think before they play, quicker. Education is the key... When you arrive at Barça the first thing they teach you is: think. Think, think, think. Quickly. [Xavi starts doing the actions, looking around himself.] Lift your head up, move, see, think. Look before you get the ball.' The bracketed stage direction is the Guardian's own. Jordet's reproduction matches. Article title: 'I'm a romantic, says Xavi, heartbeat of Barcelona and Spain'.

verdicts.claim: Eye-tracking of 4 elite Norwegian central midfielders (869 scans): mean scan 0.40 s, median 0.34 s, 90.3% at or under 0.66 s, 2.3% contained a fixation (120 ms threshold); peripheral vision does the work.
verdicts.note: Mean 39.65 cs, median 34 cs, '90.3% of all scans performed ranged from 2 to 66 cs', 20 of 869 scans (2.3%) had a fixation. Authors warn the 120 ms threshold comes from lab studies with little movement. Only 4 players, Eliteserien.

verdicts.claim: Eye-tracking of 5 elite Norwegian central midfielders in 11v11 (2,832 fixations): mean fixation 242 ms; longer fixations with more objects in view.
verdicts.note: Five central midfielders aged 17-23 (M 19.84) from two Norwegian premier league clubs, all former Norway U21 players. Two 11v11 training matches, not official matches. Mean 242.29 ms (SD 195.03).

verdicts.claim: Semi-elite players (32 men, 16-30 y, 783 possessions) head sensor: 0.95 turns/s at 10 s before to 1.44 turns/s at 1 s before; excursion predicted turning, frequency predicted forward passes; pass success not linked.
verdicts.note: Values confirmed: 0.95 (0.21) and 1.44 (0.53). Nuance: the forward-pass link held only for the 4-9 s windows before possession. Turning link held across all windows. Pass success: no association for any window.

verdicts.claim: Competitive-elite youth (22 players, 16.25 y, 1,623 min 11v11): most exploration in back third, least in middle third, more in possession, less in transitions.
verdicts.note: McGuckian et al. 2020, J Sports Sci 38(6). Abstract: 'Twenty-two competitive-elite youth footballers (M = 16.25 years) played a total of 1,623 minutes'. Australian sample. Tandfonline returned 403, verified through Europe PMC.

verdicts.claim: UEFA U17 and U19 2018 semi-finals and finals (53 players, 1,686 situations): U19 scanned more than U17; CM and CD most; positive scan-pass success link; pressure and pitch position shaped scanning.
verdicts.note: Aksum, Pokolm, Bjørndal, Rein, Memmert, Jordet 2021, J Sports Sci 39(21). All elements in the abstract.

verdicts.claim: UEFA U17, U19, U21 (239 players, 17 matches): positive scan-pass link; pressure had a large effect on pass result and body orientation.
verdicts.note: Pokolm et al. 2022, JSEP 44(4):263-271. Abstract confirms '17 selected matches and 239 players' from 2018-2019 championships and 'opponent pressure had a large effect on pass result and the player's body orientation'.

verdicts.claim: UEFA U17 and U21 2019 (162 players, 9 matches): last scan toward dominant-foot side raises the chance the dominant foot makes first contact.
verdicts.note: Pokolm et al. 2023, J Sports Sci 41(7):695-705. Abstract: 'the direction of the last scan prior to receiving the ball is related to the foot used for the first ball contact'. Note: this is about scan direction and foot choice, not about 'back foot' technique as such.

verdicts.claim: Euro 2016 midfielders (35): scan rate correlated with passing percentage, R-squared 3.0-4.0%.
verdicts.note: Phatak and Gruber 2019. Scan rate R2 = 3.0% (p = .033), total scan rate R2 = 4.0% (p = .015). Transition scan rate vs turnover rate R2 = 3.5%. MDPI returned 403, verified through Europe PMC.

verdicts.claim: Elite youth female players (25, mean 17.6 y) in 4v4: verbal cues raised scans before reception by 27% (RR 1.27, CI 1.12-1.44); at least one scan gave OR 3.40 (CI 2.59-4.62) for a successful next action.
verdicts.note: Hintermann et al. 2025, Eur J Sport Sci 25(11). Numbers match. Caution: OR 3.40 is an odds ratio, not '3.4 times more likely'. Say '3.4 times the odds'.

verdicts.claim: Heads Up Girls! (36 U19 female players, 16.7 y, Swiss): 0.88 to 1.44 scans per situation (p = 0.002), kept at retention; elite 1.06 to 1.72; grassroots not significant; 70.6% vs 62.5% positive outcomes.
verdicts.note: Table 2: intervention 0.88 ± 0.36 to 1.44 ± 0.52; control 0.61 ± 0.27 to 0.92 ± 0.43. Table 3: elite 1.06 to 1.72, grassroots 0.52 to 0.87 (n.s.). The control group also rose, so the between-group gain is smaller than 0.56. 70.6% vs 62.5% (p = 0.001) confirmed.

verdicts.claim: Elite youth female (39 players, 17.45 y, Swiss U19, 4 matches, 819 events): 0.27 scans/s before reception, 0.61 during possession, possession 1.62 s, OR 1.09 per 0.1 scans/s, tight pressure cut dribble odds 92%, timing no association.
verdicts.note: All values match the article text.

verdicts.claim: Jordet's 2005 imagery study showed exploratory behaviour trainable in a few weeks (as summarised in Jordet 2013).
verdicts.note: 2013 text: 'only a few weeks practice gave immediate increases in exploratory behavior frequency and that this for some players also produced immediate gains in performance'. Primary: Jordet, J Appl Sport Psychol 17(2):140-156, 2005. Not fetched.

verdicts.claim: Pocock et al. (2019) imagery intervention to train visual exploratory activity in elite academy players, JASP.
verdicts.note: Crossref: 'Using an Imagery Intervention to Train Visual Exploratory Activity in Elite Academy Football Players', Pocock, Dicks, Thelwell, Chapman, Barker, J Appl Sport Psychol 31(2):218-234 (online 2017, print 2019). Existence confirmed only. Results not fetched.

verdicts.claim: Ligue 1 (28 players, 30 matches): 53.4 ± 8.1 s in possession per match, 1.1 s and 2.0 touches per possession, 4.2 m per possession, 191 m per match, 10.3 km/h at reception.
verdicts.note: Carling 2010, J Sports Sci. All values match the abstract.

verdicts.claim: Bundesliga 2013/14 (60 matches): individual ball control 1:21 per player per match; central forwards 0:49; central defenders and goalkeepers 1:38; about 836 IBC intervals per match.
verdicts.note: Link and Hoernig 2017. 1:21 ± 1:13 min for players who played the full match. 836 ± 424 intervals per match. IBC = 'sufficiently under control that he can consciously chose between several play options'.

verdicts.claim: 34 boys (13 ± 0.9 y): 3v3 on 15x25 m gave more short passes, kicks, tackles, dribbles and goals than 6v6 on 30x40 m; HR 87.6% vs 82.8% HRmax.
verdicts.note: Katis and Kellis 2009. 6v6 gave more long passes and headers. 10 x 4 min bouts.

verdicts.claim: Pre-pubescent players (about 11 y): 7v7 on 60x40 m gave more passes and fewer tackles than 11v11 on 100x65 m; HR over 170 bpm 84% of the time in both.
verdicts.note: Capranica et al. 2001. Very small sample: six players in 11v11 and seven in 7v7. Treat as indicative.

verdicts.claim: Scottish Premier League (15 pros): 3v3 gave more contacts per player than 9v9 (large effect), more dribbles, shots, tackles, fewer passes, receives, headers.
verdicts.note: Owen et al. 2011, JSCR. 3v3 + GK vs 9v9 + GK, 3 x 5 min. Large-sided games also had more blocks and interceptions.

verdicts.claim: Elite players (18 ± 1 y): 5v5 pitch 30x20 to 50x40 m did not change HR or most technical actions; tackles 45 vs 15; shots 85, 60, 44.
verdicts.corrected_value: Format is not stated in the abstract. Eight players took part, so 4v4 is the likely format. Say 'small-sided games', not '5v5', unless the full text is checked.
verdicts.note: Kelly and Drust 2009, JSAMS. Abstract confirms 8 players, HR 175/173/169 bpm (n.s.), tackles 45 ± 10 vs 15 ± 4, shots 85 ± 15, 60 ± 18, 44 ± 9. 'Pitch size is a dial for pressure' is a fair reading: tackles fell as space grew.

verdicts.claim: U15 players (28 boys, about 12.9 y): experienced players built longer sequences with more circulation; inexperienced faster, individual; 3v3 vs 6v6 changed both.
verdicts.note: Almeida, Ferreira, Volossovitch 2013, J Hum Kinet 36. Experienced group had 3.93 ± 1.00 years of federation football.

verdicts.claim: Simple visual reaction time in 1,469 adults (18-65): about 231 ms (213 ms corrected), rising about 0.5 ms per year.
verdicts.note: Woods et al. 2015. 231 ms uncorrected, 213 ms after 17.8 ms hardware correction, 0.55 ms/year. Experiment 2: 189 subjects, 237.8 ms.

'High-skilled but not low-skilled players can compensate for eccentricity effects in real game situations, indicating their superior positioning and perceptual strategies.' Basketball, lab setup, transfer to football by analogy.

verdicts.claim: Coefficient of restitution definition; property of the two surfaces; no football-foot value on the page.
verdicts.note: Page: 'The COR is a property of a pair of objects in a collision, not a single object.' No football or foot value listed (golf, tennis, table tennis, basketball only). The direction of the retreating-foot argument is right: ball velocity after = v_foot(1+e) - e v_ball, so a foot retreating at about e/(1+e) of ball speed leaves the ball near rest.

verdicts.corrected_value: Numbers confirmed. The interpretive sentence overstates: a relaxed, less stiff foot also lowers the rebound (lower COR), and foot angle plus ground friction also kill the bounce. The 9 ms figure is for maximal kicks by 11 adult players, not for a cushioning touch.
