verdicts.note: All three quotes match the PDF text.

verdicts.claim: Aksum et al. (2021) practical applications: quick scans in a dynamic affordance-rich environment; limit non-contextual information (cones, numbers); limit unopposed exercises.
verdicts.note: Quotes match. Example given: 'counting the number of fingers the coach is presenting or reading a number on a sign'.

mechanism_errors: Population mix in step one: 'Premier League players turn their head about three times... Each look lasts less than half a second, and the eyes barely stop on anything.' The 3.0 scans come from 27 Premier League players (video). The 0.40 s duration and the 2.3% fixation figure come from 4 Norwegian Eliteserien midfielders wearing eye-trackers. Say 'top-level pros' or name both groups.

Causal overreach: 'Players who looked most often completed about 73 percent... The look lets you decide before the ball comes.' Jordet 2013 is correlational. The 2020 Premier League paper says the scan effect is small next to technical ability and pass difficulty. Phatak 2019 puts scan rate at 3-4% of pass-success variance. McGuckian 2018 found no pass-success link in semi-elite players. Phrase it as 'players who look more also complete more passes', not 'looking makes the pass succeed'.

Odds vs probability: 'one look before the ball already triples the odds' is acceptable, but claim 14 says '3.4 times more likely'. OR 3.40 is an odds ratio. For a kids' narration say 'more than three times the odds' or 'much more likely'.

Heads Up Girls control group also rose (0.61 to 0.92 scans per situation), so the trained gain of 0.56 overstates the pure training effect. Say 'the trained group scanned about 60% more, and kept it three weeks later'.

Rebound physics: direction is right (retreating foot lowers approach speed; ball ends near rest when the foot retreats at about e/(1+e) of ball speed). But 'only a moving-back foot can reduce the rebound' is too strong. COR is a property of the pair and of stiffness, so a relaxed ankle lowers e too, and angling the foot to push the ball into the ground also kills the bounce. The 9 ms contact time is for maximal instep kicks by adults, not a cushioning touch. Use 'a few milliseconds', not the exact number.
'Pro players keep the ball about one second per possession, two touches' is adult Ligue 1 data. Swiss U19 women held the ball 1.62 s on average. Kids hold it longer still. Label the number as pro.

Reaction time: '~0.2-0.25 s to read a move and start reacting' is simple reaction time to a light in non-athletes (213-231 ms). Reading a feint is a choice reaction and takes longer. Brault's 268 vs 193 ms is movement-initiation time after the attacker starts moving, in rugby VR. 'Expert defenders even wait longer on purpose' adds intent the paper did not test.

The 0.43 s child reaction time is unverified (Šovčíková 2015 abstract gives no such mean). The misconception line 'Kids' defenders are slower to react, so feints work even better at U12' has no youth feint data behind it. Drop or soften.

Misconception 2 clashes with the Ghent claim. Mendez-Villanueva shows between-age-group sprint differences vanish once maturity is controlled. Vaeyens shows running speed still separates elite from non-elite within U13 and U14. Correct framing: 'much of the speed gap between age groups is maturity, but skill (dribbling) keeps improving after 16 and separates future pros'.
Pressure definition in claim 2 is wrong: d = 0.57 compares 0-1 m with 10+ m, not '4 m or more'.
'98 percent contain no fixation' rests on a 120 ms threshold from lab studies and 4 players. Say 'almost never stop on one thing long enough to count as a fixation'.
Visual field: side-on puts passer and goal at about ±90 degrees, the far edge of a 200-220 degree field, where only motion registers. Say 'in the corner of your eye', not 'both in view'.
Flying 10 m at U12 (6.3 m/s) means 5 m in about 0.8 s at top speed. A defender closing from a jog needs about a second. Say 'about a second', not 'under a second'.

Manchester United '135% more passes in 4v4 vs 8v8' could not be verified (no search budget left). The usual citation is Fenoglio (2003), 'The Manchester United 4 v 4 Pilot Scheme for U9s', Insight, FA Coaches Association Journal. That is from memory, not fetched. Keep it labelled as unverified.
Rondo quote wording: both secondary sources say "'one touch' soccer", not 'football'.
safe_numbers_for_narration: Premier League pros (27 players, 9,574 possessions) scan about 3 times in the 10 seconds before the ball arrives, roughly one look every two seconds.
Pros scan less under tight pressure: about 0.38 scans per second with a defender within 1 m, about 0.46 with the nearest defender 10 m or more away.
Premier League midfielders and forwards (118 players) who scanned most completed about 73% of passes; those who scanned least completed about 54%. This is a correlation.
Premier League midfielders who scanned much completed 73% of forward passes; those who scanned little completed 38%.
Lampard and Gerrard had the highest scan frequency in the 2013 Premier League sample: 0.62 scans per second.
Elite pro midfielders' scans (Norwegian top division, 4 players) last about 0.4 seconds on average; 9 in 10 last under two-thirds of a second.
Elite youth female players (4v4, mean age 17.6) who made at least one scan before receiving had 3.4 times the odds of a successful next action.

Swiss U19 female players trained for five weeks went from 0.88 to 1.44 scans per game situation and kept the gain three weeks later; actions were positive 70.6% of the time after a scan vs 62.5% without.
Elite youth players (UEFA U17/U19) scanned more at U19 than at U17; central midfielders and central defenders scanned most.
Ligue 1 pros have the ball about 53 seconds per match, about 1.1 seconds and 2 touches per possession.
Bundesliga pros have real control of the ball for about 1 minute 21 seconds per match; central forwards about 49 seconds.
13-year-old boys in 3v3 (15x25 m) made more short passes, dribbles, tackles and goals than in 6v6 (30x40 m), with heart rate 87.6% vs 82.8% of maximum.
11-year-olds in 7v7 (60x40 m) passed more and tackled less than in 11v11 (100x65 m).
Elite 18-year-olds: growing a small-sided pitch from 30x20 to 50x40 m cut tackles from 45 to 15 and shots from 85 to 44. Pitch size is a pressure dial.
Elite youth: flying 10 m sprint is about 1.58 s at U12 (6.3 m/s) and 1.31 s at U16 (7.6 m/s).
Dutch talented youth: future pros were 0.3 s faster over 30 m dribbling and about 1 s faster on 3x30 m repeated dribbling than those who stayed amateur.
Talented youth 12-19: sprinting improves fast from 14 to 16 while dribbling stalls; after 16 dribbling improves and sprinting hardly changes.
Elite youth U14-U18: sprint differences between age groups disappear once biological maturity is accounted for.
Expert rugby defenders (adults, VR) waited about 268 ms before moving vs 193 ms for novices, and were fooled 14% of the time vs 42%.
Adults (1,469 non-athletes, 18-65): simple visual reaction time about 0.21-0.23 s.
Humans see about 200-220 degrees horizontally with both eyes, a bit more than a half circle; the sharp centre is only about 5 degrees.
A football is 68-70 cm around and 410-450 g at kick-off (IFAB Law 2, adult size 5).
KNVB: O8-O10 play 6v6 on 42.5x30 m with no published standings; O11-O12 play 8v8 on 42.5x64 m; 11v11 starts at O13.

scores.topic: Concept as written: 'Why the Best Players Look Slow' (LOOK / TOUCH / SHAPE, football is a game of time)
scores.reason: Scanning has the best field evidence of any perceptual skill in football. Jordet et al. 2020 (27 EPL players, 9,574 possessions) found a mean of 0.44 scans/s, more scans before completed passes (0.46 vs 0.40 scans/s) and a small positive Bayesian effect on pass completion (https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.553813/full). It also found scanning collapses when a defender is 0-1 m away and plateaus at 4 m, which is the physical basis for the 'time bubble'. The youth evidence is direct: at the UEFA U17/U19 Euros, U19 players scanned more than U17 and scan frequency predicted pass success (Aksum et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1935115). More head turns before receiving raised the odds of turning with the ball and passing forward (McGuckian et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02520) and made pass decisions faster (https://doi.org/10.1080/10407413.2018.1495548). Body orientation ties SHAPE to LOOK: scan frequency was related to changes in body orientation and opponent pressure had a large effect on body orientation and pass result (Pokolm et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.1123/jsep.2020-0299). It is trainable in youth: a 6-week imagery programme raised scanning in academy players (Pocock et al. 2019, https://doi.org/10.1080/10413200.2017.1395929), one session of verbal cues raised scans before reception by 27% in 17-year-olds, and one scan tripled the odds of a successful next action (Hintermann et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70070). Weak spots: I found no peer-reviewed biomechanics of receiving a ball (the first-touch chapter rests on generic bounce physics, Cross 1999, https://doi.org/10.1119/1.19229, and instep-impact data, Shinkai 2009, https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e31818e8044), and the effect of scanning is small (d = 0.15) and did not separate award-winning players from their teammates (Caso et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1080/24733938.2024.2325139). Freshness is 4, not 5: Jordet's scanning work is now popular on coaching social media, but the 'time' framing for kids is not.

Dribbling is the technical skill with the best longitudinal link to a professional career: talented 14-18-year-olds who later turned professional were 0.3 s faster over 30 m with the ball and 1 s faster on 3 x 30 m repeated dribbles than those who stayed amateur (Huijgen et al. 2009, https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0029-1202354). Dribbling improves most from 12 to 14 and again after 16, and hours of practice predict it (Huijgen et al. 2010, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640411003645679). Peak dribbling helped separate selected from deselected academy players (https://doi.org/10.1080/17461391.2012.725102). In 1v1s with 11.8-year-olds, attackers won through unpredictability (Duarte et al. 2012, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2012.675081), and step-overs reverse a defender's automatic cueing so lower-skilled defenders guess wrong more often than chance (Wright and Jackson 2014, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0104290). The problem is saturation: skills-and-moves videos are the most common football content online, so this scores lowest on freshness. Good as a chapter or teaser, not a whole episode.

scores.topic: Passing weight and leading a runner
scores.reason: Pass speed and receiver pressure are exactly what tracking-data models use to price pass risk and reward (Power et al. 2017, KDD, https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098051). Kicking biomechanics give the pass-kick numbers: side-foot foot speed 18.3 m/s vs 21.6 m/s for the instep (Levanon and Dapena 1998, https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199806000-00022). Touch limits in 4v4 raise pass counts and shorten touch intervals in junior players (Rosten et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.5114/jhk/196142). But I found no peer-reviewed study that links pass weight to the receiver's next action in youth, so the science story is thin and would rest on physics of ball roll. Drills are easy. A strong future episode if you fold it into 'time': a well-weighted pass gives the receiver the bubble.

scores.topic: Defending: jockeying, angles, reading the hips
scores.reason: Almost nobody makes defending explainers for kids, and the science is good. In rugby side-steps, expert defenders waited longer (moved 268 ms vs 193 ms before the cut), followed honest cues (centre of mass) instead of deceptive ones (trunk, foot), and went the wrong way 14% of the time vs 42% for novices (Brault et al. 2012, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0037494). In football step-overs, high-skilled players had higher sensitivity to genuine vs fake actions and lower-skilled players were biased to believe the action (Jackson et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02043). In 1v1s with 11-12-year-olds, the winning defender kept a lead-lag relation and a predictable coordination pattern (Duarte et al. 2012, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2012.675081). Williams' review covers anticipation and visual search (https://doi.org/10.1080/02640410050120113). Jockeying distance and angle drills exist in every federation syllabus. Best candidate for episode 3 because it is the mirror image of this episode: the attacker buys time, the defender steals it.

For U12 the rules remove most of the value. U.S. Soccer: no heading in practice or games for 11-U and younger, U12-U13 limited to 30 minutes of heading training per week and 15-20 headers per player per week, and an indirect free kick when a young player deliberately heads the ball in a game (https://usclubsoccer.org/headinjuries/). The FA: no heading in training in the foundation phase and a graduated approach from U12 to U16 (https://www.thefa.com/news/2020/feb/24/updated-heading-guidance-announcement-240220), and a trial from 2022-23 to remove deliberate heading from U12-and-below matches (https://www.thefa.com/news/2022/jul/18/statement-heading-trial-u12-games-20221807). I could not verify the FA's rules after that trial, so check the current season before you script anything. The health science is active but not settled: one season of youth football showed no differences from non-contact athletes in a 2026 JAMA Network Open cohort (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.19569). A heading how-to for U12 would conflict with the rules in both countries.

The anticipation science is classic: expert keepers waited longer before moving, made fewer corrections and fixated the kicking leg, non-kicking leg and ball rather than the trunk (Savelsbergh et al. 2002, https://doi.org/10.1080/026404102317284826). Kicking practice improved penalty reading in experienced keepers (Ridderinkhof et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2021.789817). But it applies to one player per team, and at U12 many teams rotate keepers. Better as a short segment inside a defending or 'reading the body' episode.

The science is strong but it argues against a speed episode for U12. A meta-analysis of sprint training in male youth found a moderate overall effect (ES 1.01) that was large after peak height velocity (1.39), moderate around it (1.15) and negative before it (-0.18) (Moran et al. 2017, https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0042-111439). Age-group differences in acceleration and top speed in academy players disappeared after adjustment for maturity (Mendez-Villanueva et al. 2011, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2010.536248). Post-PHV players out-performed pre-PHV players on every physical test (Scardina et al. 2026, https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1856821). The Youth Physical Development Model frames this (Lloyd and Oliver 2012, https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0b013e31825760ea, and Oliver, Lloyd and Rumpf 2013, https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0b013e3182919d32). Speed still matters at the top: sprints preceded about 41% of open-play World Cup goals (Daly et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70085). Mechanics are hard to teach through an animation.

Set plays produced 42% of goals at the 2018 World Cup and the team that scored from one won 71% of the time (Vergonis et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.23736/s0022-4707.20.11788-2). But the numbers come from senior football on full pitches. Youth small-sided formats have fewer corners and free kicks near goal, and the 'science' is mostly notational statistics, not mechanism. Routines are easy to drill but they age badly and do not build a player.

scores.topic: Why the biggest kid is not the best (maturation and the relative age effect)
scores.reason: The strongest science story of all the alternatives, and the one no kids' video tells. In 1,003 UK academy players, 45.0% were born in the first quarter of the selection year and 9.8% in the last (Bolckmans et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2022.847438); a Belgian sample showed 41.4% vs 14.9% (Helsen et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2021.635379). Sprint differences between age groups vanish when maturity is controlled (Mendez-Villanueva et al. 2011, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2010.536248), while dribbling keeps improving after 16 when sprinting stops (Huijgen et al. 2010, https://doi.org/10.1080/02640411003645679). This tells a late-developing 13-year-old exactly why the 'time' skills in your episode 2 are the ones that last. It has no drills, so it scores lower on teachability. Strong candidate for episode 4, or a 60-second coda to episode 2.

scores.topic: The warm-up that halves injuries (11+ Kids)
scores.reason: A multinational cluster RCT in 3,895 players aged 7-13 cut all injuries by 48% and severe injuries by 74% (Rössler et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0834-8). An Iranian cluster RCT in 962 players cut injuries by 50% (Zarei et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2019.12.001), and 10 weeks of the programme gave large strength gains in 11-year-olds (https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2018-0827). It is the only topic where the video can literally be the drill. It does not change how a player plays, so impact on the game is indirect. Good as a one-off 'do this every session' episode.

scores.topic: Small-sided games: why 3v3 makes you better
scores.reason: In 13-year-olds, 3v3 produced more short passes, dribbles, tackles and goals than 6v6, with higher heart rates (Katis and Kellis 2009, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3763282/). Verbal cues and small-sided games are also how the scanning interventions above were delivered. But the audience for this argument is coaches and parents, not the U12 player, and it is a format, not a skill.

challenge.advice:
Keep the concept. Of the eleven topics it has the best product of impact, science and freshness for a U12-U16 audience, and it is the one topic where the youth field evidence is direct rather than borrowed from adults (Aksum et al. 2021 on U17/U19, McGuckian et al. 2020 on 16-year-olds, Hintermann et al. 2025 on 17-year-olds, Pocock et al. 2019 on academy players). Nothing on the alternatives list beats it as episode 2. Save defending (episode 3) and maturation/relative age (episode 4) for later, because they extend the same 'time' idea from the defender's side and from the growing body's side.

Make these tweaks before scripting.

1. Rebuild the numbers on sources, not folklore. Use 0.44 scans per second for EPL players and 'more scans before completed passes' (Jordet 2020, https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.553813/full). Use 'a scan lasts about four tenths of a second and almost never includes a fixation, so you take a snapshot, not a stare' (Aksum 2020/2021, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0244118). Use 'U19 scan more than U17' (https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2021.1935115). Do not name players with scan counts unless you have the primary table; the public Sloan page for Jordet 2013 does not give names (https://www.sloansportsconference.com/research-papers/the-hidden-foundation-of-field-vision-in-english-premier-league-epl-soccer-players).

2. Replace 'a quarter second to react' with a two-part statement. Seeing a simple signal takes about 0.2 s in adults (213 ms corrected, Woods et al. 2015, https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00131/full). Moving the whole body takes longer, and the real story is commitment: novice defenders moved 193 ms before the cut and went the wrong way 42% of the time, experts waited until 268 ms before it and erred 14% (Brault 2012, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0037494). Teaser line: 'A feint does not beat a defender's legs. It beats his first guess.' For the defensive mirror, tell kids to watch the hips (honest cue), not the feet (deceptive cue).

3. Ground the time bubble in the pressure thresholds that exist. Scanning fell to its lowest with a defender 0-1 m away and plateaued at 4 m (Jordet 2020). Show the ring with two marks: 1 m = no time, 4 m = full time. If you show a formula, keep it visual for U12 and speak it for U16: seconds = metres of space divided by closing speed. Sanity check with youth top speeds: boys' maximum sprint speed is about 22.6 km/h (6.3 m/s) at U12, 23.6 km/h (6.6 m/s) at U14 and 26.7 km/h (7.4 m/s) at U16 (Bleeker and Siener 2025, general boys not footballers, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12714977/). Defenders close from a standing or jogging start, so a closing speed of about 4 m/s is more honest than top speed. That gives the rule of thumb 'every two metres is about half a second'. Say it as an estimate.

4. Keep TOUCH honest. The physics is sound: the rebound depends on the speed of the ball relative to the surface and on the coefficient of restitution (Cross 1999, https://doi.org/10.1119/1.19229), and foot-ball contact in a kick lasts about 9 ms with 6 cm of ball deformation (Shinkai 2009, https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e31818e8044). But there is no peer-reviewed study of the receiving touch itself, so do not print a percentage like 'a giving foot cuts the bounce by 70%'. Show it as a demonstration: same ball, same speed, rigid foot vs foot moving back. Use the hand-catch analogy. The 'one touch into space buys metres' point links back to the ring: show the ring grow when the touch goes away from Chalk.

5. Correct SHAPE. Humans see about 200 degrees or more horizontally (about 60 degrees nasal and 107 degrees temporal per eye, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field), so 'about a half circle' is a safe under-claim. But acuity halves by 2 degrees off centre and is one sixteenth at 30 degrees, while the periphery is good at motion (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peripheral_vision, citing Strasburger 2011; review of peripheral vision in sport: Vater, Williams and Hossner 2020, https://doi.org/10.1080/1750984X.2019.1582082). Script it as 'side-on, the corner of your eye catches movement on the goal side, so you know something is there, but you still need the look to know who'. Add that scanning and body-orientation changes go together in youth internationals (Pokolm 2022, https://doi.org/10.1123/jsep.2020-0299). I could not find a live FA page for 'receiving on the back foot' (the learn.englandfootball.com links I tried returned 404), so present it as standard coaching practice, not as an FA quote.

6. Age-split the drills. The one intervention that separated elite from grassroots girls improved scanning only in the elite group (Hintermann et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2025.1602099), so grassroots U12 need simple, concrete cues. Use the evidence-based cue set: before the ball arrives, look for teammate, opponent, space (https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70070). Three drills that map to the chapters: (a) LOOK: colour call, a coach shows a coloured cone behind the receiver just before the pass and the receiver calls it before the touch; (b) TOUCH: receive with a defender at 2 m, then at 6 m, so kids feel the ring; (c) SHAPE: receive through a gate on the half-turn and play forward in two touches. For U16 add the imagery script idea from Pocock 2019.

7. Frame the effect size correctly. Scanning is a small edge that costs no athleticism and repeats 40-60 times a match. Do not claim it is what makes superstars: award-winning Champions League players did not scan more than their teammates (Caso et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1080/24733938.2024.2325139). Keep the title, but anchor it in the last 20 seconds: speed still matters (sprints preceded about 41% of World Cup open-play goals, Daly et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70085); the point is that time makes speed useful.

8. Trim. Three chapters plus a bonus teaser in six minutes is tight for 12-year-olds. Give LOOK the most time (best evidence), make TOUCH the demonstration, make SHAPE the payoff, and cut the feint to a 30-second cliffhanger for the defending episode.

Confidence notes: scanning claims high; feint timing medium (rugby data, not football); youth speed numbers medium (general boys); first-touch chapter medium (physics only); FA coaching wording low (no primary page verified).

risks.risk: The 'quarter second to react' number is folklore as written. Simple reaction to a light is about 0.2 s in adults (Woods et al. 2015, https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00131/full), a whole-body change of direction takes longer, and the football-relevant finding is about when a defender commits, not how fast he reacts (novices 193 ms before the cut, experts 268 ms, Brault 2012, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0037494).
risks.mitigation: Script two numbers, 'about a fifth of a second to see it, longer to move', and make the teaser about the defender's first guess (42% wrong for novices) rather than a fixed delay. Cite the rugby study as rugby.

risks.risk: Overclaiming scanning. The EPL effect is small (0.46 vs 0.40 scans/s, d = 0.15, Jordet 2020) and scanning did not separate award-winning players from their teammates (Caso et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1080/24733938.2024.2325139). Viral 'Xavi scans 0.8 times per second' style figures have no primary source I could verify.
risks.mitigation: Present scanning as a small, free edge that repeats 40-60 times a game. Use only the published numbers (0.44 scans/s, U19 more than U17, +27% with verbal cues, one scan triples the odds of a good next action). Do not name players with scan counts.

risks.risk: The TOUCH chapter has no soccer-specific science behind it. I found no peer-reviewed biomechanics of the receiving touch, so any percentage for 'how much a giving foot kills the bounce' would be invented.
risks.mitigation: Use generic bounce physics (Cross 1999, https://doi.org/10.1119/1.19229) and instep-impact data (9 ms contact, 6 cm deformation, Shinkai 2009, https://doi.org/10.1249/mss.0b013e31818e8044) as a demonstration, not as a measured claim. Show the effect visually with two touches at the same ball speed and no number.

risks.risk: The time bubble is too abstract for 12-year-olds and wrong if built on top speed. Defenders close from a jog, decelerate and react, so 'distance divided by top speed' underestimates the time by a lot. Youth top speeds are only about 6.3 m/s at U12 and 7.4 m/s at U16 in general boys (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12714977/), and those are not football-specific.
risks.mitigation: Keep the formula off screen for U12. Use a ring with two marks taken from Jordet 2020 (1 m = no time, 4 m = full time) and the spoken rule 'every two metres is about half a second' at a closing speed of about 4 m/s. Label it an estimate. Add the 2 m vs 6 m receiving drill so kids feel it.

risks.risk: The SHAPE chapter overstates what side-on vision gives you. The field of view is about 200 degrees or more, but acuity is one sixteenth of central vision at 30 degrees off centre (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peripheral_vision, citing Strasburger 2011). A half-turned player sees the goal side as motion, not detail. Also, no live FA page for 'receive on the back foot' could be verified, so an FA quote would be unsourced.
risks.mitigation: Say 'the corner of your eye catches movement, the look tells you who', so the half-turn supports the scan and does not replace it. Cite Pokolm 2022 for the link between scanning and body orientation (https://doi.org/10.1123/jsep.2020-0299) and Vater et al. 2020 for peripheral vision in sport (https://doi.org/10.1080/1750984X.2019.1582082). Present the back-foot cue as common coaching practice, not as a federation quote.
